Hi,
Sorry if this is the wrong sub.
I have played indoor for about 2 years now, and i want to make the transition to beach. I will still play indoor, but the indoor is in their off season in Australia and i find that beach will improve my skills a lot. I just want to know any tips, tricks or even simply the culture itself before i commit to beach.
I played a couple of days, and i noticed a few things before you comment,
There are calls 1-5, left-right respectively. (also 20-50 - moving in intervals of 10, for fast tempo sets) You can call outside and behind depending if you want the player who touches the second ball to face forward or behind. In terms of defence there is a thing called a peel, where you literally do a block transition to participate in floor defense with your teammate instead of blocking. You can do cross or straight back depending on your strategy. Additionally, you can do multiple shots including hard driven, roll, cut, pokey or cobra. You can't do overhand passes unless if you do either a tomahwak or a picture perfect, no spin or no double contact 'set'. To jump approach you jump up instead of broad.
ik it seems like i answered my own question, but anything else you can add would be nice. TIA

text:
I've been trying to get a better idea of what youth club volleyball actually costs in Orange County for the 2026–2027 season, specifically for the younger 10U–12U age groups.
It has been surprisingly difficult to get consistent pricing information. Some clubs publish pricing, some only provide ranges, and some don't provide a firm number until after tryouts/team placement. Even when I have gotten pricing, it hasn't always been clear exactly what is included.
So I figured I'd share what I've been able to compile. This is not intended to be a definitive price list, and I'd really appreciate it if anyone with actual 2026–27 numbers could correct/add to it.
Approximate 2026–27 pricing
Club
Approx. base cost
What I've been able to determine
Momentous
$4,800 / $6,200
$6200 premiere team practice 3x 2hr weekly, vs 2x 2hr weekly for lower teams, they also have a $300 mandatory EOY tournament fee, 8-10 SCSN tournaments and uniform incl.
Saddleback Valley
~3,700–4,800
Club said 11U is the lowest price point. 12U-2 practices 2x/week, while 12U-1 practices 3x/week and costs more.
OAHO
$3,900
SCSN club teams. Includes training and SCSN tournaments. Travel events extra.
OAHO Local
$350/month
Non-SCSN local program. 2x/week training + monthly local events. They had 9 local teams last season.
Dime
$4,200 / $4,800
$4,200 non-Premier / 4,800Premier.Includesgym/practice,coaching,localSCSNtournamentsanduniformpackage.Additionaltraveltournamentfeescanbeupto~1,500.
AAA / Athena
mid-4,000stomid-5,000s
Current website indicates majority of teams are mid-4kforlocalSoCalcompetition/playoffs/SummerSoiree.Topteamsaremid-5k and include one out-of-town event.
Tstreet
~7,000–8,000
Parent-reported number, not an official published price. Parents I spoke with indicated player travel can be around ~$1k additional per trip, while parent/family hotel and travel is separate.
Historical Momentous pricing
For anyone interested in how pricing has changed, I also found an older Momentous 12U program from 2021 that listed:
$1,995 total
4 hours/week of training
6 SCVA tournaments
Uniform/practice shirts included
Equal participation in the tournaments
Obviously this is not a current offering, and the program structure may have changed significantly since then, but I thought it was an interesting historical reference point.
2021: ~2,000→2026–27:roughly~4,000–$5,000 estimated
If anyone has older pricing sheets from other OC clubs, I'd be interested in seeing those as well.
Important caveats
These numbers are primarily for 10U–12U. Older age groups can be substantially different.
This is also not necessarily apples-to-apples between clubs:
Many clubs have Premier and non-Premier teams
Some clubs have multiple teams at the same age level
Practice schedules vary (2x vs. 3x/week)
Practice length may vary (90 minutes vs. 2 hours, etc.)
Uniform packages differ
Some tournament fees are included and some aren't
Travel tournament fees may be separate
Player travel expenses and parent/family travel expenses are separate costs
Some clubs have local/developmental options that are much less intensive than their top SCSN teams
For example, Dime specifically quoted additional travel tournament fees of up to ~$1,500, while family travel is separate.
OAHO is particularly interesting because they offer a non-SCSN local option at $350/month with 2 practices/week and monthly local events.
It also seems like the headline price can be misleading. A $4,200 club where uniforms and local tournaments are included could potentially be cheaper overall than a $3,900 club once everything is added.
If anyone has actual 2026–27 numbers
I'd especially love to hear from parents in comments who have an actual offer/contract in hand.
If you have a daughter in 10U, 11U or 12U, please share:
Club
Age/team (11U, 12U-2, Premier or lower team, etc)
Base dues
Practices per week + approximate length
What's included (uniforms, tournaments, etc.)
Expected travel tournament fees
Whether there is a local/non-travel option
Anything else that surprised you about the actual cost
And if you're going through tryouts/commitments on October 3 and 4, I'd love to hear what pricing you actually receive.
Hopefully this helps other Orange County parents trying to budget for club volleyball. The lack of transparent pricing has made this surprisingly difficult to research, so I'm hoping the comments can turn this into a more accurate crowdsourced mega-thread and shed some light on the topic.
label: analysis

text:
This longish story but I'll give a summary at the end. For context, I'm from Italy, 23yo M
From the beginning, my first real contact with the sport was in college, where the PE major had a class any other major could join for credits. I needed credits, I enjoyed volleyball when in high school, so I joined. That my dudes was a terrible idea. People in this class were taking it repeatedly for multiple semesters and they were very good. Some were new to the sport as well, so the class was very mixed. Because it was technically an intermediate (there were no men's beginners), we went straight into defense tactics and 5x1. Honestly it was kinda of for fun, mostly games, very brief drills, because most of the guys were there to play and have fun and the teacher knew that. I fucking sucked and despite some of my class/teammates being kind and understanding, I still felt like I was just bothering them (And no, I couldn't drop the class because this was my last semester to earn said credits, believe me, I thought about it every time).
6 months later, I'm graduated, with time to fill after college was done eating my soul and I decided to do it right this time and join a beginner's team to learn fundamentals. I was very upfront about my lack of skills when contacting the volleyball "school" in my town. They're paid classes, with good teachers. They said they were starting a beginners class soon. So I joined.
HOWEVER, I found out that they were actually rebooting a class that had like a year practice before. And it's pretty clear that they are way above my level. like 80% of them have very good passing and sets, still beginners but they clearly are familiar with the sport in a way that I'm not. So I'm once again the worst stupid fuck in my team. And now, my teammates are mostly teenagers and they're not exactly being patient with the ones who are actually just beginning. And I'm not sure I can blame them, lately
Now, I assume every "beginner" team is going to have someone who's been playing for a year or two. Not everyone is like me starting from scratch. But I still feel like I'm once again being a menace to my team, that my learning process is too slow and I won't ever catch up with them. When I'm passing or setting, the ball goes where I want it to about 40% of the time, which fucks everything up obviously.
I realize volleyball is a hard sport, there's so much information being pumped out because the teachers are in a rush to get us playing tournaments (since half of the class has seen this super beginners stuff already) and I'm just overwhelmed trying to absorb everything, while my teammates complain every time I forget my position or complain that I'm not "trying" hard enough when I don't perform an action to their satisfaction (when in reality, I'm just... stupid?). All this just makes me want to fuck off this team and give up the sport even tho I look forward to it every week.
TLDR Even in the beginners class, how do you get over the feeling that you're falling behind on skill level compared to your teammates who've had a head start ? How do you fight the voices in your head telling you to give up? I know I don't want to stop playing but at the same I feel like I need to take one for the team, let's say, and fuck off like they probably want me to.

I don't make short texts, so TL;DR: Played for 5 years, I did enjoy volleyball but it makes me feel frustrated and anxious most of the time and I stopped actually having fun a long time ago.
I'm just looking to rant here. But maybe some advice could be nice.
I have been playing volleyball for 5 years, I started in the first year of high school because I wanted to socialize with the girls my age (I have social anxiety and I am generally pretty shy), but I ended up loving the sport itself.
I remember that, when I started, I would have anxiety attacks in the middle of practice because I was a complete newbie, while the girls were already on the school's competitive team (I am not from the US, so we don't have this whole deal about sports in school. We do have some competitions, but it doesn't carry that much importance), and oh boy they would be impatient with me. But I continued, I wanted to be better, I wanted to be good in this sport.
Well, fast forward to now: I started to have classes in club volleyball during my second year of high school and I did have some great moments with volleyball, I do remember some days I would make great passes and great attacks, and I even introduced the sport to dear friends of mine and they loved it. However, these good moments were quite uncommon. Most of the time, I would feel frustrated or even anxious about my form, my passing, my positioning, etc and I would try to practice as much as I could to be better.
I thought maybe the club I was in was the reason of my frustration. But I have went to every single possible place that offers volleyball classes in my city (Yes, literally), I tried participating in my university's volleyball team, but I would still feel anxious, I would still feel like I wasn't enough. You're probably thinking "Hey, stop trying to be perfect, stop trying to be so hard on yourself and enjoy this sport!" But how can you enjoy this sport if your teammates visibly get irritated with you when you make a mistake? How can you deal with that constantly? How can I have fun like this? And it's not like people would behave like this in one place only, it seems like you have to act rude towards less skilled players while playing volleyball.
I don't think these 5 years were worth it, I don't think I have gained anything from volleyball. I didn't make friends (Realized that, no matter how much you "put yourself out there", it's still you, and I am naturally not really sociable), I feel stagnated in my skills, and I stopped actually having fun with volleyball a long time ago. text:
On a recent trip to Tokyo, my daughters and I played 4v4 ビーチボール (beachball not beach volleyball) at an Open Gym in Koto City.
Beachball is a volleyball variant developed in Japan in 1977 as a less intimidating version of volleyball. It's played with custom made beach balls which are well balanced, bouncy, and strong. The game is 4v4 and played on an indoor doubles badminton court (smaller than a beach volleyball court) with a 1.8m/5'11" net.
Last time I was in Tokyo, a beachball player explained all the rules to my daughter and I so when we went to this open gym, we knew most of the rules. As with many open gyms, the players were a bit wary of us at first, considering we didn't speak Japanese, but they warmed up to us quickly when they realized we knew all the etiquette around shoes (courts are considered indoors so you only wear indoor shoes or socks on courts, no outside shoes) and we clearly understood the basics of volleyball.
For warmup, we played 2v2 then 4v4. Since we had 9 players, the 4v4 game was played with the player who made the last mistake being subbed out. There were many polite arguments about how we should be subbing out but as foreign visitors and my daughters being kids, they often allowed us to stay, taking the blame for our mistakes.
The players were diverse: A younger 20 something to some older players in their 50s. One player had only played 3 games before another had been playing for 30 years. One interesting thing about all Japanese open gyms is that a player who is sitting out refs with a scoreboard and electronic whistle and is expected to actively call nets and other violations. I haven't seen this in open gyms where I live.
Because of the low net height, I got to block! Turns out even if I can get over the net, I suck at blocking. I got tooled multiple times and had the ball dribble down on my side. To be fair, beachball has a rule that you cannot contact the ball with any of your body parts crossing the plane of the net so you have to be more conscious when blocking. Because of the low net, fat ball, and no breaking the plane rule, some of the jousts were really cool with both players standing there, pushing the ball, trying to make the ball go to their opponent's side.
It was a blast smashing downballs as slow dropping sets let me read the defense and choose my targets. Coach's half arm swing hits worked brilliantly with that ball and the ball can be hit really hard and fast but it slows down at the end of flight. My daughters, who have not played much with beach balls or badminton birdies, had a harder time adjusting to the suddenly slow down of the ball but I adapted quickly.
Serves were wild. Spin serves dominate though one guy demonstrated float serves which also gave me fits. Sadly, the best players were all holding back to make the game more fun but I saw some practice serves that moved 3-4 feet horizontally left and right and some top spin serves that dropped like they were rocket propelled.
Overlap rules are simplified with 2 players having to be left of the mid-line of the court and 2 players to the right but front back overlap is the same as volleyball. Serves must occur behind the service line and serve receivers must start behind their service line which is the badminton service line. Serve Receive formation is roughly a rotated rectangle. The general strategy was to have 3 players blocking at the net and only 1 player playing back row defense, though, watching higher level play on YouTube, it looks like they have 2 blockers and 2 defenders. Middle blocker is the setter, the other two blockers are generally the hitters but the back row defender can also attack without restriction.
The game is a blast with the beach ball generally being slower and lighter (one handed passes are easy) and thus more forgiving, leading to some crazy fun plays, but expert players can generate some insane offense and serves.
I would love for beachball to take off in other countries, especially for beginners, as it's just easier to play than volleyball. It's kind of like pickleball versus tennis. Players would need a badminton court, a modified net that allows it to be raised higher, and beach balls (which are super cheap: The high end ball is under $4.00 USD.)
After we finished playing, we learned that almost half the players spoke quite good English and we chatted about how we found the game, how long we had played volleyball, and chatted about beachball tournaments. During the game, I don't think we realized how much English everyone spoke, so we mostly used pointing and simple words like "setter" and "hitter" and "defense" and a lot of pointing but even that worked out well.
Overall, playing beachball was one of the highlights of our trip to Tokyo. We had only meant to play for an hour and we stayed for all 3 hours. The other players were very kind and welcoming and I was glad to play something so fun and uniquely Japanese while being able to tap into our love of volleyball.
EDIT: Sorry I couldn't film our gameplay! Filming was prohibited at the Sports Center. Here's some random YouTube footage of the game played at high level: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5uN8TQ6VwvQ

Today I played with a 19 year-old, who asked me if I think he can make it to become a pro, and I honestly had no idea how to answer him.
I play in the 4th german league, so well above average for amateur players, but still pretty far from pro. This kid, around 180cm tall, definitely on the talented side, could maybe play two leagues below me, more likely 3. He had a very good spike and serve, but definitely some issues with reception.
Do people just not know what pro volleyball looks like? You have to compete with kids your age who are playing second and sometimes first league, are 2m tall, have practiced this sport for 10+ years, have perfect receiving/setting technique, and usually at least some international experience, having played in youth national teams most of the time.
I really, genuinely do not want to discourage anyone from becoming their best self, and having ambition is great! Practice as hard as you can, and set your goals high! But at some point, I feel like all realism goes away. How can one have this conversation? How should one as a more experienced player react to this?
I see these posts here from time to time of kids in their late teens who started playing this sport not too long ago and fell in love with it asking, if they can make it pro. And then people sometimes give examples of pros who also started late, who are almost always extremely genetically gifted like Velizar Chernokozhev (215cm tall). My emotional reaction is to scream that they are delusional, but maybe that is just me being old and bitter.
At what point becomes ambition delusion? Can one have a realistic view and still push oneself to become a pro? After all, for all existing pros the chances were slim at some point, yet they made it.

text:
Every Turkish national team tournament ends with the same argument, so I sat down and wrote the ranking out with criteria instead of vibes: national team results first, individual awards second, years at the top third. Only players who wore the senior national team jersey count, which puts Melissa Vargas in and leaves Ebrar Karakurt out, since she plays outside hitter for Turkey now.
The list starts with the youngest name on it. Defne Başyolcu is 20, 193 cm, and spent the summer of 2026 as the second opposite in the squad that won the VNL, then picked up Mediterranean Games gold a few weeks later. She has no individual award yet and that is the honest reason she is fifth. She is also the only player on this list whose best years are clearly ahead of her.
Aleksia Karutasu, born in Bucharest in 2003, was the youngest professional in the Romanian league at 13 and moved to VakıfBank at 15. In her first VNL with Turkey, in 2025, she was the top scorer of the opening week with 91 points. Then the roster math caught up with her: Turkey has one slot for a naturalized player, Vargas counts as domestic since 2025, and that one slot goes to Sinead Jack-Kısal more often than to her. At club level she keeps producing, with the 2026 CEV Cup at Galatasaray and a 28-point match MVP in game one of that final.
Meryem Boz is third, and her case rests on one evening more than on any medal, although she has those too: bronze at Euro 2017, silver at VNL 2018 and Euro 2019. In the Tokyo qualifier of January 2020, Poland reached match point three times in the fourth set of the semifinal. Boz killed all three, Turkey won in five, beat Germany the next day and went to its first Olympics since 2012. She was named MVP of the qualifier. The club years that followed, the 2021-22 treble with VakıfBank and back-to-back league titles with Fenerbahçe, are almost a footnote next to that.
Neslihan Demir is the reason the word "opposite" means something in Turkey. She wore the national jersey from 1997 to 2016. At 19 she led the team to Euro 2003 silver, the country's first international medal outside the Mediterranean Games. She finished the 2010 World Championship as top scorer, did it again while Turkey took bronze at Euro 2011, carried the flag at the London 2012 opening ceremony as the first Turkish woman to do so, and was named an FIVB Hero the same year. Nobody else on this list, and arguably nobody else in Turkish volleyball, stayed at the top for that long. That is why she is second and not fifth, and also why she is not first.
Because the trophy count is not close. Melissa Vargas came to Fenerbahçe in 2018, chose Turkey while playing there, became a citizen in 2021 and waited out the FIVB two-year rule. Her first tournament in the national jersey was VNL 2023: title and MVP. Euro 2023 that summer: title and MVP. In 2024 she was top scorer of both the VNL and the Paris Olympics. In 2025 Turkey took World Championship silver with Vargas as best opposite and top scorer. In 2026 she put 33 points on Brazil in the VNL final, more than anyone had ever scored in one, and then won the European Championship in Istanbul as MVP again. Four tournaments, four MVPs. That is the ranking.
My own objection to my own list: if you weight longevity above trophies, Neslihan is first and I would not argue hard. Vargas also walked into a team that was already a contender; Neslihan built one from nothing. Tell me where you would put the top two, and who your fifth is.

So my u21 boy's team won our first match of the season and for some of us the first official match period (including myself) we've been training hard non stop even during summer break we were playing beach volleyball everyday and even attended a couple of tournaments during that time. And we all got a little bit hit in the feels because we've been working together for this for the past 6 months. We went from being a bunch of voleyball idiots to a full fledged team partly thanks to our great coach and partly because of our relentless passion for the sport.
So here's how the match went We go in the hitting lines flexing our best moves me as a Middle i told my setter to set me tight in order to go show off our quick attack bounce to position 4. I know trying to intimate the other team is childish but they were asking for it. Their libero came to our locker room right before the match to tell us that they were gonna go easy on us and that they wanted to end this quickly (what a fucking douchebag)
First set : So anyways we went in received the ball and got the first point but it was all down hill from there because we kept doing stupid mistakes and missing receives we were pretty nervous so we lost the first set by a huge margin something like 25-7
Second set : our coach tells us that he believes in us and that we should cheer up and go prove ourselves so we go in with a fiery passion we were screaming and cheering for every point we were getting aces stuff blocks and i was really dominant at the middle position our setter gave me a shit ton of sets during this set and i was feeling unstoppable so much so that they stopped setting their middles entirely becuase i kept blocking them . Our opposite and the outsides were on fire as well and our libero came in clutch lots of times so we easily beat them 25-17.
Third set : we go in with the same mentality and we even said that we were going in to win it. We played well and got the lead but we struggled a lot with receiving their setter's serve becuase so they racked up points and a few missed serves and a couple of mistakes later we lost by the slightest of margins 23-25.
Fourth set : pretty much the same as the second we were unstoppable at the net and their blocks weren't effective against our attacks. they mostly got points of block outs and our mistakes so we win this one around 25-19 and go to the fifth set
Fifth set : we were pretty nervous but kept being aggressive energetic and cheerful supporting each other on every point. We were leading 2-3 points for most of the time though a couple of lucky aces and missed receives later we were tied and they even lead 9-7 we changed sides and just couldn't go home without a W We were hungry and we were going 120% a couple of great plays later its 11-12 and I'm serving im not a safe player so i go for a hard hybrid jump serve as i normally do and hit that thing like my life depended on it its an overpass we get the ball and our opposite smacks it down the line getting us a point i love this dude what a life saver . 11-13 and I'm Serving i know that if i miss I'm out becuase our libero was going to sub in the back row so this was my last chance to make an impact i serve before the whistle blows becuase i didn't hear it from all of the cheers in the crowd so i serve again straight into the net 😭 making the score 12-13 (i was so bummed out about this one becuase i knew couldn't d go in to make up for it since surely the game would end in the next 3 rotations). We lose the next point and we're tied 13-13. Thankfully we receive well and get the next point by a block out from our second outside the shortest player in the Team btw 174cm (5'8.5)who's normally a libero buy he earned the position becuase our other outside didn't come to practice and was a little bit cocky. He goes in ..... IT'S AN ACE WE WIN THE MATCH We cheered and screamed out loud we had won. and we got emotional not gonna lie 😅
On a personal level I was happy that i finally proved myself on the court because I've been fighting real hard to become a starter and i finally did. I was told by my team mates coach and spectators most of which i don't know who they are that i was the backbone of the Team and that i was really dominant in the court and i could sense that i got into their blockers heads when i went up for a first tempo even if most of the time the ball wasn't going to me so our wings were left with 1 blocker and got lots of points this way. I stepped over the service line a coupled of times and got a few net violations but overall for my first official game i would say i did pretty well.
So that was my ramble about our first official match and win of the season thanks for listening to another voleyball idio like myself i appreciate you and thanks for all the tips that this thread has provided me 🙏

text:
One of the things about volleyball that make it so accessible, at least from my perspective as a referee, is that there are very few strange or unexpected rules. It’s far from, say, American football, with its immense compendium of penalties and minutiae. 98% of volleyball is pretty simple: in, out, touch-out. However, this does make the very few exceptions of particular interest to me — and my favorite of all (as some longer-time r/volleyball users may know) is the libero set rule.
For the uninitiated or curious, here’s the backstory: When the libero position was first added to volleyball about 25 years ago, one of the concerns was that a team might use it not as intended — as a defensive specialist opportunity, perhaps for a shorter player — but as a full-time back-row attacker or back-row setter. So two rules were implemented to protect against this: 1. The libero can never attack the ball above the height of the net, even from the back row, and can never even attempt to block, and 2. If the libero uses an overhand finger set from the front zone, the next contact cannot be an attack across the net from above the height of the net.
The wording here is important. The libero can hand-set, but they have to stay/jump from behind the attack line in order for the attacker to strike from above the net. In front of the attack line, the libero can still bump set or punch-set, just not overhand set with fingertip action. And the libero can even still use a hand-set from in front of the line — but the next contact must either be to a teammate, or stay below the height of the net.
Here’s a great collection of legal libero sets, including both hand-sets from behind the attack line and bump-sets from in front of it.
Faults that break this rule are of interest to me for a few reasons. They’re rare, and they often catch teams and spectators by surprise. They’re also very easy for referees to miss, so there’s some pride in catching them on the rare occasion when they happen. And in particular, teams often forget that this fault still applies even if the libero set is the first contact, or from a one-handed fingertip set. (Whether this should be the case is open to debate, but the rule is what it currently is!)
Over the past year or so, I’ve been collecting a list of example videos of this rare fault — just because, don’t judge me — and figured I’d share my collection:
The prototypical example of a libero set fault. From a college game. Note the couple of spectators in the bottom right and the coaches in the top left who start waving their arms in the illegal-attack signal — folks who know their rules!
Another very standard example, although this one is from a libero outside the court — but clearly still in front of the attack-line extension. Inexplicably, the referee ends up overturning this completely correct call; it’s never made clear why.
Fault correctly called on a back-row attack. Front row or back row — the rule is the same.
This is perhaps my favorite video of this fault. At higher levels, this is the most common way for this fault to occur: a libero takes a free ball with their hands, then a front-row setter does a surprise dump. As seen here, players often react furiously to this call at first, thinking that the referee has forgotten that the setter is front row (the illegal-attack signal is the same!), which often produces some comedy once they realize what has actually happened.
Another example of the same post-call comedy. The ball doesn’t have to be spiked — a hand-set dump is still a fault if it’s above the height of the net after a libero set in the front zone. Watch #8 howling in protest that she’s front row, even as the libero, #7, suddenly realizes what has happened and turns away in self-disgust. (You may question whether this ball really was 100% above the top of the net, but the ref decided that it was.)
They always think the ref has forgotten who is front row. Great work by the referee to be prepared to catch this on the surprise second-contact attack. Refs need to be on alert the moment they see a libero hand-set in front of the line, first contact or second contact.
... because it’s very easy to miss this call. Here the ref appears to whiff on what should have been an illegal attack due to libero set.
Another missed call. This one is rather shocking to me — an international ref should always catch this fault. I’m also very surprised that nobody else seems to spot it.
This one is rather interesting. I am not 100% sure what the FIVB rule is/was regarding a simultaneous joust after a libero set — it’s a real edge case! I believe that USAV recently changed this rule so that this would be play-on. However, in this case, the referee eventually calls the illegal attack.
Two more good examples of dump-on-two faults. We can’t see if the referee catches these faults, but both should certainly be called.
Here are two plays from the same game, both called correctly. In the second video, you can see that the attacker stays below the height of the net, and thus the attack is not a fault.
Another example of great refereeing here. The libero clearly sets in front of the line, and the black team’s coach (upper left) clearly sees that and calls for an illegal attack. The ref indicates with an informal “hand pressing down” motion that he believes the ball was at least partially below the top of the net — so no fault — which instantly placates the coach.
Finally, here are a few examples from my own games that I’ve saved:
Clear fault that I called from the R1.. I really appreciate the white team’s setter here in the upper right, who spots the fault as well and starts calling for it right away. The coach spots it, too. (Note that I am using the NFHS/women’s-NCAA signal for an illegal attack, with the arm facing forward, not to the side.)
Another clear fault that I called, this one from a boys’ game. The libero doesn’t quite stay behind the line when setting. I like his “ah, drat” reaction to the call.
A fault that I identified, but my partner did not call. As the R2, when spotting a potential fault of this type, the correct action is to hold up a “suggested illegal attack” signal to your chest, allowing the R1 to then decide whether or not to call it. Here, even though I make a big show of it, my partner doesn’t appear to spot my suggestion, and lets play continue. I think that I then make a mistake: the R2 is actually empowered to blow this fault if the R1 does not wave it off within a reasonable amount of time, but I give up on it (there is a high-powered assigner present and I get scared about embarrassing myself). The other team wins the point anyway, after which I make another mistake and have a completely unnecessary conversation with my R1. This was a good teaching moment for myself as R2 and one I still think about often!
I hope someone finds this collection of videos as entertaining as I do, and/or helpful regarding the libero set rule!
(Finally, one little bonus: my respect for Haikyuu! grew immensely when I saw them use a quick cut to show a libero taking off from just behind the attack line in order to set. That’s some intense attention to the details of the sport!)

text:
"Hey guys I'm new to volleyball, I was wondering if you could help me with my jump topspin serve?" "Hey guys I've only played for 6 months but every time I try to jump serve I can't seem to get it over but I can get my standing serve over 63.27% of the time, what's wrong?" etc. etc.
Whilst I appreciate and accept that people like to learn new things and that jump serving is a pretty cool aspect of the game, the number of times I've seen new players try to jump serve, get frustrated when they can't do it very well, proceed to ask for help and someone has to explain that it's not wise to try to learn the jump serve too soon is staggering.
As such I thought I would compile the best reasons and explanations I can think of at the moment in the rest of this post for people to link to but please feel free to list your own reasonings and experience in the comments!
1. Jump serving is a very involved movement
Jump serving is a skill that combines some of the most complex and easy-to-mess-up skills of the game. You must first toss the ball to an accurate and consistent height and distance, then you must do your approach from behind the ball without running under it, then you have to broad jump and swing at a high contact point with enough force to send the ball over the net whilst maintaining good awareness of the opposite court and the accuracy to pinpoint to any seam or gap you choose. If any of these skills are lacking, the serve will fail or won't be very difficult to receive, and even worse could have a negative impact on the rest of your skills as you try to compensate which could lead to injury or bad habits. For example if someone tosses too far left when hitting right handed on a jump topspin serve, they'll have to either compensate with their approach and risk leg injury or compromise their swing and risk their shoulder.
2. You'll develop bad habits in your spiking
With such a high skill density, the jump serve is not a safe place to learn the fundamental skills required to pull it off. The swing should be practiced on it's own, as should the approach, as should the toss. By the time you get to the toss, you should have hit so many balls and done your 3 step approach so many times that you could do them perfectly on 0 hours of sleep after a 12 hour shift. If this is not the case, any bad habits that form in your swing and approach that aren't corrected immediately will transfer to your spiking, since you are essentially trying to learn how to spike at the same time as you're serving. Once you have a bad habit, it's very difficult to get out of it so it's best to take learning complex skills one step at a time.
3. The standing serve is the perfect eco-system for learning how to swing
Yes you are still tossing the ball, but not very high and the ability to shift your feet easily to adjust for a bad toss means that a standing serve is basically all about your swing. If you can't get the ball over 100% of the time and get the ball to where you're aiming like 90% of the time on a standing float, you still need to practice your standing floats. Same goes for a standing topspin but there's less use for that serve in actual play, I would recommend learning it though if only to learn the difference in follow-through and hand position required between floating and topspin serves. And as an aside, yes you need to be able to aim your float serve before you move on if you can't aim it all that tells me is you don't actually have full control over your armswing yet, the best you can do is swing and pray, and that's far from the level of mastery required to move on.
4. Jump topspin serves aren't even good unless you can hit it hard and accurate
Jump topspin serves are used in high level play as essentially a trade-off; they accept that they'll have a slightly higher serve error percentage but in turn they can throw off and intimidate the opponent with extremely fast and hard driven balls. The key here is that they are getting power in return for consistency, but if you have no power to begin with, the jump topspin is a terrible serve. Float serves on the other hand are super consistent, whilst being harder to receive despite lower ball velocities thanks to the unpredictable floating properties of the ball. So in a game setting, a pin-point standing float will get ace after ace after ace. That's not to say that a jump float doesn't have significant advantages though, but it will be a much smoother transition to the jump float if your standing float is already close to perfect.
tl;dr learn standing float -> jump float ->-> jump float hybrid ->->-> mayyyybe jump topspin
Again feel free to add more in the comments if I've missed anything. Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk, hope I helped!
Edit: Thank you for the awards, glad it resonates!

text:
Welcome to Mythbusters: Volleyball Edition!
Like most anything on the internet, there is a lot of “knowledge” around volleyball that you’ve maybe heard in person or seen online that maybe you’re wondering the validity of. How many times have you been told to snap your wrists if you hit goes flying out the back of the court? How many arguments have you gotten into with someone who said that your set was a double because it spun? In this post, I’m going to try to answer some commonly asked and controversial questions we see around the community. Let’s begin.
=========================================
Myth #1: To get better topsin when hitting or to hit the ball in, snap your wrist
This is one of the most common pieces of advice that gets thrown around anytime someone is struggling to bring the ball down into the court. “Just snap your wrist”. I hear it from newer players, veterans, and everyone in between. But just what is the truth on this?
In reality, snapping your wrist will not get you better topspin for a better hit. On a powerful hit (aka not a rollshot or something), snapping your wrist does not impart significant enough spin to change the trajectory of the ball. The contact time of the hand and ball is simply too quick to matter. So what exactly can you do to get topspin on the ball? How can you get your ball to land in the court and not 5 bricks up the back wall?
[This graphic](http://i.imgur.com/G6S2JRp.jpg) shows a basic breakdown of how to generate topspin. Topspin is generated by hitting through the ball above the center of gravity IN RELATION TO THE DIRECTION OF MOTION OF THE BALL. I do mention that this is all in relation to direction of motion because I don’t want you to imagine “above” as being “above” relative to the parallel plane of the ground. For instance, in the bottom 3 images, the direction of motion of the ball would be almost straight down on the left-most image, about 45 degrees downward in the middle image, and relatively straight or a few degrees upward in the right-most image.
So now that you can do a killer topspin, how come your balls are still landing out of bounds or aren’t bouncing as sharp as you would like? Topspin isn’t going to make a huge difference if you’re looking to hit downward more. It can if you’re hitting from off the net/low position and you’re trying to paint the back line but if you’re already comfortably above the net, and can’t seem to control the ball, topspin won’t do it.
In 99% of cases of someone hitting the ball out constantly or weakly compared to where they should be, the issue is being underneath the ball.
Take a look at[ this graphic](https://imgur.com/a/jjG8qlE). No amount of topspin is going to save the first hitter. Topspin may save the 2nd one but it’s going to be less powerful than the 3rd hitter. And in the case of the 3rd hitter, no amount of topspin or lack thereof is going to cause the ball to alter path. If you’re struggling to get good power and downward movement even though you’re up above the net, take a look at what your body/arm looks like at the point of contact. Keep that ball in front of you.
So are there situations when snapping your wrist is useful? Definitely but they tend to be unique situations. In offspeed rollshots, snapping your wrist can impart some extra spin on the ball due to the longer contact period between your hand and the ball. It also gives you more control of the ball.. Another situation is when the ball is super tight to the net and you can’t swing through as much as you would like. Changing the angle of your wrist can impact the direction the ball goes and can allow a more downward hit than normal but sacrifices some speed and power.
=========================================
Myth #2: You should not follow through on your float serve
This one hits close to home because it’s actually how I was taught to serve way back in the day (middle school). In fact, I’m sure many of us were specifically coached to stop your hand at the moment of contact to get that perfect float serve and that’s what we’ve done for years.
In fact, following through on your float allows more power/speed and will still result in a float when done correctly. If you watch any pros or higher level players execute a float, no one will stop right at the ball unless maybe they’re trying to drop it in front of the 10’ line. So why were we all taught to stop our hand at the point of contact?
When learning to float serve, taking away the follow through can let us practice visualizing the point of impact on the ball and get immediate feedback on how our serve went. Learning the way to contact the ball for 0 spin is crucial at this point rather than speed. Once you’re familiar with hitting through the center of gravity of the ball (remember that earlier graphic?), feel free to add follow through and increase the velocity of your serve. You’ll see a huge difference.
=========================================
Myth #3: Setting should be done with the fingertips
I’m not sure how or why this one gets propagated so much. As a setter, it drives me absolutely bonkers hearing this being taught to young players. In fact, I play with a pretty decent player who coaches varsity at her local high school but her sets are all off of her fingertips and they are just ugly. I have no question that she is teaching her kids the exact same thing.
Setting should be done with as much finger area as possible. The ball should be contacting almost up to the palm on at least 4 of the 5 fingers (some people use pinky, some don’t).[ Here is a graphic](https://i.pinimg.com/originals/c7/40/1f/c7401f396fd28f46efe8a5dd34e2670c.jpg) that really highlights how much of your fingers should be touching the ball. This increased surface area drastically increases the control you have over the ball and allows a smoother transition of force from your wrist to the ball.
Here are some more photos of some setters.[ 1](https://riccaj.weebly.com/uploads/3/0/0/4/30048525/6906758_orig.jpg),[ 2](https://a.espncdn.com/photo/2017/0821/r247138_4_800x450_16-9.jpg),[ 3](https://www.teamusa.org/-/media/USA_Volleyball/Images/2019-Articles/January/010119ChristensonSet800x500.jpg?h=auto&w=100%25&la=en&hash=AFD68D6CE65E84D629FAE601DFE5E422B51A6FEA),[ 4](https://i0.wp.com/setupforvolleyball.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/How-is-Volleyball-Played-set-1.png?resize=640%2C360&ssl=1),[ 5](https://rdrhpwb.weebly.com/uploads/2/6/9/2692385/8824740_orig.jpg). Notice how deep the ball sits in their hands and how the fingers contour with the ball to maximize that contact area. There isn’t a single good setter who uses their fingertips to set and neither should you.
=========================================
Myth #4: Setting mainly comes from the legs
This isn’t really a myth but more of an understanding issue. In short, younger setters who are learning to set will learn to use their legs for power simply because their forearms aren’t developed enough to use their elbows and wrists alone. As setters progress, they will switch to be more forearm/wrist focused. For a setter to jumpset, almost all of the power comes from the forearm/wrist as you can imagine. Hard to use leg power when your legs are just dangling in the air.
Generally, the more advanced a player you are, the less you will rely on your legs. However, this is not to say that good or even great setters never use their legs to power a set. Botched plays, scrambles, and all sorts of miscues can force setters to use their legs to add that extra oomph to their set to get the ball out a bit further.
=========================================
Myth #5: Passing/serve receive is controlled and powered with the legs
Leg control vs arm control in passing has been a relatively recent shift. The old school of thought was to keep your arms pretty much locked and let your legs control the pass. But if you really think about it, this doesn’t make much sense when we look at how passers have to react and adapt to hits and serves coming in at velocity.
Your arm muscles in general are very highly tuned and can adjust the speed and direction of a ball quicker and more precisely than your legs. Your arms are simply much better suited to take power off or add power to a pass than squatting up and down at different intervals. They can also easily twist and shift for redirects whereas your legs will just kind of clumsily try to turn your entire body. Your arms can also kill the power of a high speed hit or serve when necessary. Try doing that with your arms locked out.
In general, while you can’t neglect your legs when passing obviously, your arms will be the main guiding force behind your bump. They are way more capable than your legs at adjusting passing force and direction.
=========================================
Myth #6: I need to bend my legs backwards when hitting
If I asked you to draw a person hitting a volleyball, we’d all probably draw something similar to[ this](https://i.redd.it/lmno85ogrwu11.jpg). The legs will generally be in a bent up position that we all know and love. In fact there are probably very few high level players who don’t look like this photo when smashing a ball into the court but what exactly is going on here?
This “myth” isn’t really a myth but it does pop up as a question that gets asked a lot. Some players are concerned that they don’t look like this photo so they try to consciously bend their legs to look like the picture.
Bending legs midair generally is a “natural” result of broad jumping slightly into your hit and having a solid armswing with a good cocked position. As a player gets more comfortable with hitting from a high position (you do need some form of vertical to have enough time to be loading like this), they should see that their legs automatically bend backwards to counteract the shift in your center of gravity from the “cocking” of the hit.[ Watching in slow motion](https://youtu.be/FMtUqoxfR50?t=26), the swing happens in sync with the legs kicking out. All of this combined together equates to a more powerful swing. Imagine if I gave you a huge sledgehammer and told you to do a running jump swing at a target. You’d probably look a little something like[ this](https://tonecap.files.wordpress.com/2014/11/300-sword-meets-whip-xxl.jpg). Same idea really.
In essence, bending your legs is something that will come naturally with a strong approach, decent vert, and solid armswing mechanics. It’s not something that you need to “work on” to improve but if you’re not seeing this in your swing, I would take a look at what part of your approach/swing is lacking.
And no, bending your legs does NOT let you jump higher.
=========================================
Myth #7: Spin indicates a double contact when setting
This one is probably the most argued over rules in beach volleyball. It’s even bleeding into indoor a little bit but thankfully not much. Good thing this is a very easy myth to bust.
In no official rulebook anywhere, is spin called out as a fault. No rule that says if it spins more than half a rotation, it’s a double. Nada. In fact, the USAV beach volleyball rule states “Rotation of a set ball may indicate a held ball or multiple contacts during the set but in itself is not a fault.”
BUT in reality, without proper officials with good line of sight and a proper understanding of the rules, setting an arbitrary “spin” rule may just be a simple way to self ref amateur games.
[Here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bPWw-UxS1d8) is a great video that explains the faults in beach setting.
=========================================
Myth #8: Volleyball shoes are the best shoes for volleyball
One of the most popular questions on this subreddit is “what shoes should I buy?”. If you’ve read these threads, you’ll notice that a lot of people are actually suggesting basketball shoes rather than volleyball shoes. Simply put, the R&D money going into basketball shoes eclipses the money in volleyball shoes. The movements and requirements of both sports are pretty similar with a lot of emphasis on traction, cushioning, and support.
That’s not to say that volleyball specific shoes aren’t great but when researching your next volleyball shoe, take into consideration some basketball models as well. Although at the lower end of the budget ($50-80), it seems like there are more volleyball shoes available.
One issue I’ve noticed with basketball shoes is that because new models come out just about every year and there is such a huge selection, trying on and comparing all the models is quite a pain in the ass. Also, basketball shoes are discontinued and refreshed every year meaning that sometimes the model you want is just impossible to find for a reasonable price.
=========================================
Myth #9: You are too old to start learning volleyball
Well not right now right now maybe because a lot of gyms and such are shut down but ANYONE can start learning volleyball at any time. Yes you may be behind some of your friends who started earlier but with enough time and effort, it’s possible to get yourself up to a competitive level. Will you make the varsity team with no experience prior? Probably not but hey, you never know unless you try. At worst, you spend a couple of days exercising and at best, you find a new life long passion to pursue.
=========================================
Myth #10: You can go pro
Frankly? If you’re reading this right now, you probably aren’t going to be able to become a professional player. Pros began training at young ages and even then, they are already the best of the best. And even the best of the best don’t all go pro. If you’re here on Reddit taking advice from chumps like me, chances are, you’re not going pro. Sorry.
=========================================
Myth #11: Haikyuu! is good
Just kidding. Haikyuu is great. No spoilers please!

My (I'm a first year coach) 5th grade team is going to the school league championship! We relied on two skills to win: Scrambling defense (what we lack in ball control we make up for with athletic movement to save shanks) and fast serves (for 5th graders) which get us 10-15+ aces/winners every set.
Here's the issue: Most of our fast serves look like baseball pitches. Nobody else in the volleyball community serves with our form anymore. In fact, 3 separate club coaches (during group classes) have told my daughter her serving style needs to be "fixed": less baseball pitching more standing float.
I get what they're saying: Standing Float, Jump Float, Hybrid, or Jump Top Spin are likely the future serves everyone is going to use. "Baseball pitch" serving is not one of those with a good future.
However, "Baseball Pitching" serving got us to the championship. This raised some questions to for me:
* How does a physically weaker person (like a 10 year old) generate enough power with the "standing float" style swing to get the ball over the net? I ask because my 8 year old daughter is being coached to standing float but she is just so weak the ball barely goes over from the 10 ft line. Does a physically weak U10 have any chance of standing float style serving over the net from the back line? Can she improve her technique enough to do it or does she just have to get stronger?
* What are your opinions on kids learning "stop gap" techniques like "Baseball Pitching" serves that only work at a certain age group, then the technique gets "aged out" as the kids get older? The players are ecstatic they made the championship but if I had guided them away from "Baseball Pitching" serves early in the season, they likely wouldn't have made the championship. And it's not like I intended to teach them "Baseball Pitching" serves. They just couldn't get standing floats over the net so I encouraged them to speed up their arms... and they borrowed from other sports and each other.
* Should I have tried to teach them a jump float which would have been useful going forward but also would have added a little bit of heat to their balls? Is teaching a jump float to a 10 year old in 8 weeks a totally losing proposition? Or just encourage weak standing floats which are "correct" but essentially a game losing tactic?
Anyway, we hope to win the 5th grade championship game with "baseball pitching" while our opponents weak standing float without float serve at us. It feels slightly wrong but I can see why "baseball pitching" is appropriate for volleyball inexperienced 10 and 11 year olds... even if it is a stop gap at best and a dead end which has to be unlearned at worst.

Lots of beginners don’t know what to work on, here are the entire list of skills that is used in a match and what professional volleyball players work on.
3 Phases Include:
* Serve Receive
* Offense
* Defense
Serve Receive Phase
Serving:
* Progression: Standing Top Spin, Standing Float, Jump Float, Jump Top Spin, Hybrid Float-Topspin
* Training Variable: Toss, Approach, Jump, Arm Swing, Contact, Aiming
Receiving:
* Progression: Right Handed Top Spin Receive, Left Handed Top Spin, Float Receive
* Training Variable: Shuffling, Depth, Platform, Angle, Falling Skills
Rotating, Rotation System, Stacking:
* Understanding Clockwise Rotations: Understand 6 Zones of a volleyball court, how everyone rotate when they score a side out point
* Understanding 4-2/5-1/6-2 Hitter-Setter System
* Understanding Stacking: How to position players effectively without overlaping, have the desired numbers receivers, hide setters/front middle/essential hitters for offense,
Offense:
Set:
* Progression: Bumb set, Standing Set, Out of System set, Jump Set, Delayed Jump Set, One Hand Set, Fake Spike Set, Dump, Wipe,
* Training Variable: Footwork, Hand Position, Location, Precision, Tempo
Spike:
* Progression: Line, Angle, Deep Angle, Sharp Cut, Tip, Tooling, Back Row, Show and Take (Wrist Away and Cross Body)
* Training Variable: Approach, Jump, Arm Swing, Aiming
Offensive Transition:
* Learn different Combinations, Receive-Offense Transition , Defense-Offense Transition, Covering
Defense
Blocking:
* Progression: Block Line, Block Angle, Show Line Block Angle, Show Angle Block Line, Ball Blocking, Wide Blocking
* Training Variable: Footwork, Positioning, Multiple Blockers Landing
Digging:
* Progression: Diving, Pancake, Scoop Defense, Show and Take Positioning
* Training Variable: Positioning, Platform, Hip Depth, Falling Skills
Defensive Transition:
* Serve-Defense Transition, Offense-Defense Transition
Bonus Skill: Split step, almost a reflex of a pro athlete, you will see athletes take splits steps during all skills like receiving, digging, blocking, setting, spiking approach
Volleyball is not easy, it's not a girly sport, it's complicated, explosive, breath-taking and hard to watch as non-players. Knowing all the phases and fundamental skills help you analyze a player and how he play his/her game better. Watch professional indoor or beach player and you will see that all their foot &amp;amp; upperbody work is precise, consistent and powerful.
Good Free Online Resources For Research:
* Karch Kiraly
* Eric Shoji Youtube Channel: Receiving and Digging
* Dustin Watten Youtube Channel: Receiving and Digging

text:
I’ve been seeing a lot of posts on here asking for advice on how to jump serve. I’ve also been teaching a lot recently and have noticed some trends among new players learning to serve. I thought I’d share some insights and advice that might help you guys out!
When I first got into volleyball, it was because I’d seen one of my friends jump serve at a casual game we were playing. I honestly thought it was the coolest thing in the world and obsessed over it for a month, digging up any tutorials I could find, pestering everyone in my life who knew how to do it to teach me, and practicing like crazy every day. However, after weeks and weeks of hard work, I just couldn’t seem to get it...
What I’m trying to say is that I get it. Jump serves are really cool; I still think that. However, I learned the hard way that there are some prerequisite skills you should probably master before you start trying to learn how to jump serve.
Now, I’m sure you’ve probably heard that before. The whole, “you shouldn’t start jump serving yet” speech, but hear me out. I have no doubt that you could probably learn to hit a jump serve with enough determination. If your goal isn’t to use it in a competitive volleyball environment (as in you just want a cool skill to mess around with), this approach is acceptable and you can probably stop reading here. The serve’ll eventually get to a point where it’ll go over the net and maybe even look super cool, but without the basics mastered, it won’t be a good serve.
A lot of players I’ve taught start with the goal of getting serves over the net consistently. That’s a great goal to start with, but I feel that too many people make this their end goal. Think about this for a second: why did volleyball serves evolve from underhand, to overhand, to jump serves?
Because it looks way cooler!
True, but there are other aspects behind this. Power for one, but also more nuanced advantages such as control over spin and accuracy.
If you just want to make sure your serves consistently go over the net, just learn how to underhand serve. I’d go as far as to argue that underhand serves can be quite competitive, especially at lower levels of play. Skyballs are always decently effective, and it’s fairly easy to get underhand serves to float and move around. Furthermore, the fundamental mechanics of an underhand serve are extremely simple. It’ll be relatively easy to learn and master.
Now, if you’ve read that and realized serving over the net isn’t enough, you’re getting on the right track! Keep this in mind though: you still need to CONSISTENTLY serve over the net and in the court; it’s just not an end goal anymore. It doesn’t matter if you have a 70 MPH jump serve if you miss 75% of them, right?
Similarly, don’t serve to just get the ball in play. When I serve, I serve to ace. That is my sole goal. I know that sounds obvious, but really make that a concrete goal. Stop settling for just getting the ball in. Again, it’s expected you do, just make it a goal to take it further!
Now, you’re ready to start on your journey learning how to effectively jump serve! It’s time to choose which style you’d like to learn:
The Topspin Jump Serve: these serves are typically faster than floats. They have a downward spin (or topspin, hence the name) which causes the ball to move towards the ground slightly faster. This is the serve typically referred to as the “jump serve”.
The Jump Float Serve: these serves aren’t usually quite as fast or flashy, but are typically a more effective serve in game. The ball is hit with no spin, which causes it to move around mid-air. This makes it usually more difficult to pass
Almost everyone I’ve talked to finds it easier to pass a good jump serve rather than a good jump float, however, exceptional jump serves can be more effective at high levels of the sport. For this reason, I would recommend starting with the float (I did this as well); remember you can always learn the other serve later on!
Now that you’ve chosen your serve, the basic process for learning the serve is pretty similar between topspin and float.
* Start with the standing version of the serve! It’s extremely important that you learn how to hit good topspin/floats and it’s unnecessarily difficult to try to do this jumping. You have enough other things to worry about. Instead, take some time and get really good at hitting the standing versions of these serves. Consistency is key!
Also, when first learning these serves, I highly recommend focusing on getting the correct spin on the ball rather than getting it over. What I mean by that is having a serve that consistently floats but goes into the net is significantly better than a serve that goes over but never floats. The first scenario is just a matter of adjusting your aim upwards a bit as opposed to having to learn how to float.
* After you have MASTERED your standing serve, there are two more skills to master before you should start tackling your jump serve. The first is your approach and the second is your toss.
* Practice your approach without a ball. Learn all the steps and the jump. Become extremely comfortable with this to the point that you could do it in your sleep. Once this is done, combine it with the swinging mechanics you learned from your standing serve. It'll feel silly to swing at empty air over and over again, but trust me, there's no point hitting a ball if you can't do it with the proper technique. It'll just build bad habits and make it significantly more difficult for you in the future.
* Once your approach is solid, practice just tossing the ball. Again, I know it sounds stupid and like a waste of time, but it is near IMPOSSIBLE to hit a good serve with an inconsistent toss. Go through your approach, toss the ball as if you’re going to serve, and catch it at the point you plan to hit the ball. Again, you should be able to do this in your sleep before you move on to the next step.
* You’re there! It’s time to learn the jump serve! Put the approach and toss together. It may take a few reps, but the process of combining the two should be fairly straight forward.
Now, you can hit your serve, probably with considerable power. What next? Start with adjusting the trajectory of the ball. You want your ball to pass just a foot or two over the net every time you serve. This will not only give your opponents less time to watch and pass the ball, but it'll allow you to hit harder since the ball will have a better chance of staying in the court.
Finally, start training your aim. Be able to pinpoint any spot on the court and serve directly at it. I think this just comes with lots of repetition.
Here are a few more tips for maximizing the effectiveness of your serves AFTER you've learned to hit them consistently.
* When you're in game, watch for weaker passers. This seems obvious, but really pay attention to who you want to serve next.
* Aim at lines on the court (side, back). This leaves the opponents less room for error.
* Aim at the seam between two players, especially if they're weaker passers that you've identified.
I know all of these sound pretty obvious, but they do really help when serving.
This is by no means a comprehensive guide on how to learn to serve. There are a plethora of videos on the internet that do a fantastic job of that (I'd recommend the "How to SERVE a volleyball" series from Elevate Yourself). This was meant more to provide insight and advice on how to proceed about learning to serve and the mentality that should come with it.
I hope that this helped you in some way. I'm by no means perfect and still have a lot to improve on, so I'd appreciate any comments or feedback. Furthermore, if you've got any questions, I'd be happy to answer them!

Its an intense practice match against a local university team. Our club was already ahead slightly and our outside just slammed the ball on a clean side out.
I rotate to position 1, it was my turn to serve. I wasn't exactly feeling confident today, but the ball seemed to fit my hand nicely while hitting against the wall.
I take my usual 6 steps back from the service line, breathing in and out slowly to control my performance anxiety which I always faced playing against other teams.
I do my routine, and toss the ball high. It felt just right and I jump. Still holding back slightly from being scared of missing on my first serve, I hit the ball with around 70% of my strength. A loud slap signifies a perfect contact and the ball dips hard just before it reaches their left receiver. It was an ace, but not a satisfying one.
The ball comes back, and I go for another. With more confidence in my steps, I did my routine exactly the same, and the toss was slightly lower than usual. Risking it for the biscuit, I put everything into the hit and contacted it slightly to the right, adding a tiny bit of spin that curved the ball right between position 1 and 6. They fumble and the ball ricochets off their hands and far behind them.
I went again, but this time the toss was way too forward. I jump horizontally into the court as much as I can and prayed I didnt step on the line, pushing the ball lightly and rolling it between the middle and opposite not partaking in the serve receive. They panic and they go out of system, forcing them to push it high over to their outside. A monster block by our middle allows me to go again.
Three more rips and three service aces later I was exhausted. Thats 6 points in a row and 3 aces in a row. My heart was pumping and the adrenaline was flowing through my blood.
Using the remaining strength I had, I tossed the ball high and into the court, forcing myself to reach for it and I barely managed to. With a full swing the ball flew higher than I thought, but was going incredibly fast. Everyone expected it to fly out, but it dips perfectly into the edge of the end line and that marks my 6th service ace in a row. I roared with my ego boosted beyond belief and my team cheered with me. It felt amazing. I havent made any plays like this in months and it revived a part of me.
Then I got too tired, did a standing float and their opposite crushes the ball on a sideout.
Worth.
(Source: The very match I had hours ago)

text:
Today's post is probably going to be one of the favourites that I post to this sub. It's something underutilized that's starting to creep into elite level play but there's absolutely no reason that some mid to high level players shouldn't be picking it up and that's the 2 man serve receive.
If you're a libero that's comfortable passing outside your body and have an outside that you trust to do the same this can be such a game changer.
As the name suggests this involves each player taking half the court and will obviously only be practical for float serves.
Benefits include:
Killing confusion- you now only have one seam and it's covered by the libero, it makes it so much easier to react off the ball when there's only 2 of you that are responsible for passing it.
Better passers- by taking your weaker passer out of the receive this allows you to have your two stronger passers receiving every ball. Obviously you'll be having to move a bit more but I've found that the payoff is worth it if the passers are proficient.
Mental load on the server- it puts a shitload more pressure on the server to know that you're confident enough to take their serve without a 3rd man.
Court feels less crowded- this one is subtle when you think about it but extremely noticeable on court but opening up the pass to only 2 passers leaves them feeling much more free in their movements.
Bring the libero back in to the game- libs will know the pain of not being served for the first 2 sets and going cold. This is heavily mitigated when the lib is brought in to cover over half the court. If you're a lib and you're not passing on serve receive what is the point of you even being on the court?
Opens up your other outside hitter- with your other outside hitter out of the pass they're free to play the sideout like an opposite, this can be gigantic against teams whose strategy until now has just been to serve the outside in 4.
Let me know what you think of this one and how it's worked when you've tried it. I find that coaches and teams can often be scared to deviate from the norm but the game is evolving pretty fast these days and the best players and coaches think about why we do the things we have always done and what's the next step to make it better.

text:
How many times have we heard something like- 'If you aren't putting top level pace on the ball, a jump top spin serve is a poor decision compared to a float serve'
Especially on the internet, every time someone posts a video of their jump serve there is usually some comment about the speed and how it would be ineffective in a game.
I went to an open tryout for a NVA (the small American pro league) team over the weekend. 40 high level guys in the gym, many of whom were D1/2 experienced or had overseas pro experience. There were also a handful of locals like myself. I'd say I'm an AA/A player and really went for the experience. Plenty of us non D1 guys were getting aces and out of system passes with our jump serves.
While I was obviously cut, one piece of feedback I got from an assistant was that my serve was 'slower velocity but absolutely effective' (he must hang out on the serving form threads on this subreddit) Guys like myself were getting aces against the pro players all night. Vice versa, not every serve from an experienced pro was a guaranteed ace.
Stop worrying about how hard your jump top serve is.
Instead, worry about your form and placement consistency.
What I noticed most about the effectiveness of the serves were the following- Any serve that was an ace or resulted in the receiving team being out of system was most often passed outside the midline/body of the passer, IE they were reaching to one side or another with their platform. Also, most aces or OOS passes were from balls played either short of the passer, or higher up on their body, by their shoulder level. So serving slightly deeper or shorter vs serving right at the passer was immensely effective.
No matter if it was a bomb of a serve or a mid level speed serve, if the passer was able to get their body to the ball, passing accuracy was much better. One of the hardest hitting guys had an unfortunate habit of serving directly at the passers and so he was not getting the amount of aces in which people who value speed over everything would claim he deserved.
To clarify, I am not saying that weak serves are not weak. I am saying that an effective jump serve only needs to be hit hard enough so that, when coupled with good placement and ball flight trajectory (not a rainbow but a line drive, which does not require top level power), a passer cannot both track and move their body to the ball before having to pass. It is my opinion that the power required to accomplish this is much more common than top level only.
So you're working on your jump serve- optimize your toss and approach, contact the ball at the peak of your jump, aim for deep sidelines. Know how deep the average serve receive is going to be and make sure the ball is at their shoulder height and either to their left or their right, not directly at their waist.
TL;DR- An effective jump serve only needs to be hit hard enough so that, when coupled with good placement and ball flight trajectory, a passer cannot both track and move their body to the ball before having to pass. It is my opinion that the power required to accomplish this is much more common than top level only.
