text:
I don’t know what the situation is outside Italy, but here we have really bad sports news. Of course, soccer dominates the scene in an almost dictatorial way, but that’s not even the worst part. Soccer news, in fact, rarely cover topics such as game or team analysis, focusing instead on the latest tweet of player X or the latest Instagram pic of player Y’s wife that “drove the internet crazy”. In this depressing environment, there have been a couple of exceptions. The most prominent one is “[l’Ultimo Uomo](https://www.ultimouomo.com/)” (literally “the Last Man”), a sports website clearly inspired by now-defunct Grantland. Soccer is the dominant topic there as well, but their posts are interesting analysis of games, squads and players or tales about the past. Also, there’s an entire section dedicated to NBA basketball and another one to various sports. Volleyball is rarely covered, but there’s a very competent writer named Gian Marco Porcellini who is a pleasure to read when he writes about volleyball. His[ latest post](https://www.ultimouomo.com/wilfredo-leon-nuova-pallavolo/) is about how Wilfredo Leòn is changing volleyball. It’s a deep technical analysis of his game and I thought many people here would be interested, so I contacted the author and he gave me permission to translate some of his work here. I’ll skip most of the statistical analysis because I covered it many times in my posts, so I’ll focus on the more technical paragraphs. Beware, it’s a VERY LONG article for today’s standards (my translation is about 1,600 words long) but, hey, there’s a reason why they like Grantland! I just hope that, since they’ve been recently bought by Sky Sports, they won’t do to l’Ultimo Uomo what ESPN did to Grantland.
SPIKING
Leòn is 201 cm tall (6’ 7”) and can spike as high as 385 cm (12’ 7”), only Kaziyski (12’ 9”) can do better in Superleague. What makes him unique is his ability to avoid the block, despite using only a finite set of solutions and despite attacking in a relatively intricate and slow manner.
The quality of the pass, the speed of the set, the attacking zone, the run-up. None of those things matter. Almost 6 times out of 10 he will kill it, often with a cut shot that goes over the block or by its side. The blockers don’t matter either, because Leòn can tighten the cut even against 3 men and kill it in front row, with powerful and precise balls that no one can dig.
Thanks in part to De Cecco, Leòn is often able to fully extend his arm and hit the ball neatly at its highest point, creating trajectories that even the spectators can’t follow. Also, the very few times in which he goes for a lob or a whiff, the ball is hard to dig as well, because the back row is expecting the ball to go long and stays at the edge of the court.
With faster sets, closer to the antenna, Leòn prefers to hit on 6-5, mainly to anticipate the block, but he doesn’t need second tempos to avoid the block. In fact, in order to jump higher, charge the extra shoulder rotation and having more options available, he seems to prefer more arched balls, closer to third tempos.
In situations like those, the block should have an extra fraction of a second to position and invade. Leòn, instead, exploits those situations to float in the air, delaying the spike and offsetting the block timing. It’s like he and his opponents are part of the same video, but with different speeds.
Modern volleyball is getting faster and faster, with powerful hitters who try to anticipate the spike to outpace the block-defense. Still, Leòn is so dominant on a physical level that he almost seems to go on the opposite direction, slowing down until the very last moment. He loves the cut shot, but he can opt for a line shot when he’s 1 on 1, the setter is on front row or the block allows it.
While everyone is focused on Leòn’s huge athletic talent, we have to acknowledge his volleyball IQ as well. One of the reasons he’s so efficient on cut shots, in fact, is that he has great dexterity and kinesthesia, which allow him to target unguarded spots. In fact, among Superleague spikers, Leòn has the lowest attack error ratio, just 10.6% and well above Juantorena’s 11.9%.
Despite his spikes being (theoretically) predictable, it’s hard to read Leòn, also because his run-up doesn’t change significantly when he’s preparing either a cut or a line shot. For example, when he’s in 5 and doesn’t receive, he goes a few inches left outside the field, ending the run-up with the left foot, which is barely inside the ground the moment he jumps. It’s not the feet movement that directs the spike, but his instead his pelvis rotation.
Leòn is efficient not only from 4, but also on bics and pipes, a solution that De Cecco chooses often on counter attack. Leòn prefers the extra rotation when on front row, but on back row he tends to opt for direct 6-to-1 spikes. Lately, he’s been very efficient from 5 as well, in order to help Perugia escape P1, a solution that is rarely used in modern men’s volleyball.
SERVING
His deadly service is executed in an almost robot-like sequence. Leòn always starts from 1, about a meter inside the court, and hits along the run-up. Every other aspect is a constant. The jump height, the ball toss, the leap that allows him to hit at the apex and almost inside the 7-8 meters, and the jolt that “wraps” the ball, keeping the arm well extended for maximum power.
Usually, Leòn targets the middle of the ground and rarely looks for the lines. This means that, other than looking for the receivers’ overlap zones, he basically doesn’t change the arm’s rotation degree. Sometimes, when he’s on a series, he may choose to target a different receiver.
Most servers possess a wider set of choices than Leòn, making them less predictable but also increasing the error ratio, since an out-of-run service aimed at the lines does not follow the natural biomechanics and lowers both power and precision. As for his spikes, Leòn always follows a very precise pattern, probably due to an almost obsessive training ([here](https://youtu.be/mR961CtSiY0?t=192) you can watch him serve with a GoPro mounted on his head).
Among his many aces, there’s one that got stuck in my mind. On November 11th, against Modena, Leòn had just scored an ace with an incredibly powerful and precise ball that hit the ground just left of Urnaut. On the next serve, he threw a meteorite that equaled Zaytsev’s speed record (134 km/h), once again on the Slovenian OH who got hit in the chest. It almost looked like Urnaut didn’t even think about receiving that ball, but instead used his chest to protect himself, pretty much like when Wile E. Coyote opens the umbrella to shelter himself from that giant boulder.
Since his arrival in Superleague, Leòn has kept an insane ace ratio, much higher than in the past. In the last 4 Champions League seasons, he averaged 2.73 aces/match. He ended this season with 3.76. Also, he doesn’t miss much, 143 errors and 94 aces for -0.12 efficiency and a 1:1,52 ratio. His Italian Superleague record is 7 aces against Monza, while in last year’s Russian Superleague playoffs he got 10 against Kemerovo.
OTHER FUNDAMENTALS
It may look odd that such an excellent players in those fundamentals is so below average in the others. Still, volleyball underwent through a very high specialization in the last years. All-around players like Ngapeth or Kovacevic are the exception, not the rule. That said, it’s a pity that such a physical player is so weak on blocking, especially on reading, delaying the jump and helping the middle.
Leòn is 27th for blocks/set among Superleague spikers, with a 0.20 average. His OH buddy, Lanza, who doesn’t have neither the body nor the technique of an élite blocker, averages 0.25. In reception (16.7% perfect, 5% efficiency), he has problems dampening the ball with his legs and directing the pass. Also, when he has to flatten down, he tends to lose balance and kneel instead of keeping steady and land on the side.
He faces the same problems on defense, where he’s pretty bad on covering the space behind the block but at least average in position defense, in which he tries to get hit on his upper torso. The 2nd touch is way below average as well, since he often opts for a very predictable bump set without any creativity.
PERUGIA
In order to make room for Leòn, both on budget and on the lineup, Perugia let Zaytsev and Russell go, signing Lanza instead. The former Trento captain inherited the Tsar’s burden and he has to cover a lot of ground on reception, given Leòn’s poor mobility. Lanza had ups and downs this season, with decent numbers on offense (48,8% kills, but only 381 spikes. Leòn had 573, Atanasjevic 638), not so much on reception (20.6% perfect, 11% efficiency). His numbers are way worse than Zaytsev’s and even worse than Russell’s (21.8% perfect, 12% efficiency), who was the “offensive” OH. Those numbers should not be a surprise, however. Lanza and Colaci represent 2/3 of the Italian NT back row, who suffered a lot on reception and defense in the last WC against tough opponents.
Perugia looks like a bigger-scale Leòn, with ridiculously high kill % and ace ratio, but way below average reception (and blocking, if I may add). Its fortunes depend largely on him and Atanasjevic, who, in terms of highs and options width, is now the best OPP in the world along with Sokolov. The Cuban and the Serbian, together, score 56.2% of Perugia’s points and represent 60.0% of its spikes.
If the consecutive Atanasjevic-Leòn service turn doesn’t break havoc or one of them is below par, it gets very hard for Perugia to win. Perugia lost 3 times this season (against Padova, Monza and Trento). In all of these games, Atanasjevic never went over 45.8% kills, while Leòn had 48.3%, which is decent but way below his par, especially when his team has so little alternatives on high ball.
Aside from the difficulties in organizing the right spacing between blocking and defense, Bernardi often complained about how the flow gets interrupted when the sideout phase doesn’t work. After the win against Ravenna in December, he talked about “frequent, almost constant amnesia that can be very dangerous”. After the 3-0 defeat against Trento, first and (so far) only defeat against a top team this season, he said that “we’re having a hard time dealing with mistakes or good plays by our opponents, we’re a bit fragile”. Finally, after the tie-break win against Verona, he urged his players to “fill in the gaps”.
There’s an upside to all this, though. Perugia can afford to be less structured than other teams, to play a predictable volleyball and to be less effective on sideout, because they can rely on two excellent attackers and on a setter like De Cecco, who can turn any dumpster ball into an easy kill for the spiker. Perugia is the 2nd best team for break points and the worst for sideout points, and that says a lot.

I believe this may have some merit because the faster a ball is moving, the less time it’ll have to float. However, air resistance is proportional with velocity, so the likelihood for the ball to float and the magnitude it does so should be greater. Furthermore, even if a ball doesn’t float as much, having it move a small amount going faster seems more effective than a large movement at a slow speed (although a well aimed float across seams would be devastating, even at slow speeds).

Lil history of me(21M) and vball: I’ve never played in a club and I’ve taught myself most skills, from youtube videos, or learnt from friends who used to play in clubs. Been playing regularly for about 2 years with generally a fixed set of people. I’m 175m tall, and play outside or opposite when we do play with positions.
My vertical is decent, as in, if I fully jump without spiking I can get ~~head and shoulders~~ top half of my head above the net. For reference, I can just barely touch the rim of a basketball hoop.
Ive always had a problem with my spike timing, if I get a set, I would either lob it cus ik my timing is bad, or hit it into the net. When I do have to spike while paying attention to the set, I tend to jump lower, probably due to mental stack and lack of repetition.
Then one day I met this guy who had great form, and invited him to a friendly 3v3 indoor session for fun and to get some reps in. I decided to record the hitting line that we did in the session (I think thats what they call hitting training right?)
The tips for spike timing
After that training I looked at the video frame by frame to compare my form to his, and I found a few pointers.
1. In the initial part of my approach, before swinging my arms back, I kinda flail my arm around, mostly because I didnt know what to do with them. I also thought you had to swing your arm forward and high to swing them back with more power, but thats not the case, and unnecessary. I looked at the guy’s form and he kinda just keeps his arms relaxed and low before swinging back.
2. I didn’t swing my arm back enough before my jump, and outwards (which is energy wasted). Watching his form compared to mine made me realize that I can swing my arm backwards with more power, and more for efficient energy conversion to the jump. I started swinging back my arms parallel to each other and I could instantly feel the force difference between the two, resulting in higher jumps.(although a quick note, you do need to have some shoulder mobility to swing them back and high)
3. I noticed, right after my jump and leaving the ground, I jump with my hitting arm already pulled back. I should have both my arms extended upwards, according to the guy’s form at least. This makes sense because it results in more efficient force conversion into your jump.
Now you might think all of these tips are related to the jump, what does it have to do with your spike timing? The jump technique actually matters a lot for spike timing, at least it did for me, I could jump higher, meaning higher contact point, and more angles to choose from when attacking. It was also less effort to jump as high, meaning more free brain power to focus on the actual hitting.
Before I always felt like I couldn’t jump as high when I jump for a spike. Somehow everything just came together after I brushed up my jump technique, I could more easily spot where I had to jump and where to hit, and jump higher to reach the point of contact.
Now I am working on hitting it at the right time more consistently(at the middle point of my air time), and hitting harder with focus on external hip rotation and proper pullback and arm swing.
Additional general tips
This section is for tips that float around this subreddit and tips that are recommended often that I think are relevant.
- Hit in front of you, not on top of you. I’ve been told this many times but it never registered in my brain. After hitting against the wall, for a while, I realized hitting in front of your shoulder instead of on top of your shoulder provides more strength and control.
- For a 4 step approach, have your 1st step already ‘planted’ and ready to unleash your 3 final steps when the setter touches the ball, change your speed/pacing of your approach according to how high and where the set is. (I only know the timing for 4 step approach cus thats what I am used to)
- Proper arm swing mechanics, make sure you are ‘whipping’ the ball instead of pushing it. (there’s a lot of videos out there that probably explain better than I do, so I won’t go in detail here)
- Proper and explosive penultimate jump (a lot of videos and reddit posts about this, won’t go into detail)
- I’d recommend recording your form and ask someone who has good form if you can record theirs, to compare them side by side, you’d be surprised how many mistakes you’ll find.
Conclusion
All in all, my volleyball journey continues, but I am happy with the progress that I am making so far. I hope any of these tips helps at least one person out there.
Any additional pointers and corrections to my suggestions are welcome.

Italian Superleague - match day 12 recap
SUMMARY
Last face-off in the first half of the regular season between two Scudetto contenders, as in Trento, the newly-crowned World Champions faced Modena. Let’s start with the important stuff. I’m happy I had the chance to meet[ u/DanielAviationPhotos](https://www.reddit.com/user/DanielAviationPhotos/) in person! He’s a really nice guy, for some reason I thought he would be older than he is. We also had a selfie together to put on Reddit but it turned out awful so for our sake I decided not to post it. Now, let’s talk about the game. Trento had their full roster, while Modena had to force the recovery of Holt because Mazzone reported a microfracture in his cuboid bone, so he will be out for a while. Modena started strong in the 1st, but every time they were able to gain a 3-point lead, Trento came back and tied the set. Modena got the first set ball, Trento managed to cancel it as well as the following one but, on the 3rd attempt, Russell got blocked and Modena got the 1st. In the 2nd, it was Trento’s turn to start strong, but Modena reacted immediately and the set was tied at 5-5. A very tight set with a lot of lead changes. Modena went up 22-20, then Kovacevic’s turn at the line changed the game. First he forced Modena to a negative reception with the jump float, then he changed to a spin serve and scored 2 aces, giving Trento 2 set balls. Anzani cancelled the first, but then a net fault by Holt tied the game 1-1. In the 3rd set, Trento leveled up, especially on defense, and dominated the set until 18-11. Modena then slowly started to come back and, on 23-21, had even the chance to cut the deficit to just one point, but Zaytsev spiked out, giving Trento 3 set balls. Modena cancelled the first 2, then Russell took advantage of an ill-placed block by Modena scoring the definitive 25-23. Not much to say about the 4th set, which Trento dominated 25-20 and which closed the game 3-1. 3rd defeat in 3 matches for Modena against a Scudetto rival and, once again, huge regrets. They had the 2nd set, but got stuck again on an opponent’s serving turn. Had they waken up earlier in the 3rd, they could have won it as well. But, in the end, they lost again. Those games showed exactly why, in my pre-season power rankings, I placed Modena under all the other Scudetto pretenders. Their starting lineup is the weakest among them, mostly because they lack a consistent OH2. Kaliberda (9 points, 28% kills, 16% efficiency, 1 ace, 1 block) was bad again, but for some reason Velasco didn’t give Bednorz anything but glimpses in the 2nd and 4th set. It wasn’t just Kaliberda’s fault, though. Zaytsev (20 points, 46% kills, 2 aces, 2 blocks) had his worst game of the season in terms of offensive efficiency (34%), Holt (7 points, 40% kills, 1 ace, 2 blocks) is still far from his best condition and Christenson, while having 63% positive reception and 41% perfect, is still reluctant to run bics and pipes. What really worries me, though, is Modena constantly taking an advantage then turning into the Night King from Game of Thrones, lifting its arms and resurrecting the dead. On the other side of the net, Trento started slowly but then showed some great things. Kovacevic (21 points, 49% kills, 3 aces) deserved the MVP because he changed the 2nd set pretty much by himself, but I would have probably voted for Grebennikov. 81% positive reception, 41% perfect and, most of all, some crazy defenses that kept Trento alive and forced Modena to attack with a global 43% kills despite a more than positive reception. Russell (20 points, 51% kills, 1 ace, 1 block), as always, was able to hid the n-th bad performance from Vettori (9 points, 36% kills), while Lisinac (10 points, 75% kills, 4 blocks) was positive as well.
Perugia went to Sora (actually to Veroli, but never mind) to avenge the defeat against Padova and, most of all, to defend the 1st place in the standings. They seemed to be on the road of doing so when they took a 21-19 lead in the 1st, but then Sora turned the table around with Petkovic and an ace from Joao Rafael won it for the home team. So, Perugia lost the 1st despite Sora’s 38% kills, scored just one point from the service line and recorded 9 errors in that fundamental. What do you do? It’s simple, ~~you kill the Batman~~ you score 9-f*cking-aces in the 2nd set alone and you win 25-16. Perugia added another 5 in the following 2 sets and took home a 3-point victory that didn’t seem so easy to gain after the 1st set. 12 of Perugia’s 15 aces were equally divided between Leòn and Atanasjevic. Perugia had 63% kills and nobody under 58%. They still looked like a team that doesn’t really know what to do if their ace machine stops working. On Satuday, it was Marco Camperi’s last game as Lube's head coach, with De Giorgi’s future team hosting Castellana. Stankovic was preferred to Simon (who set on the bench the whole game) but, other than that, it was the usual lineup for Lube. Castellana got a 6-points lead in the 1st, then Lube woke up, turned the set around and won the set 25-22. The home team seemed in control of the match on 10-5 in the 2nd, then Castellana started creating problems to Lube’s reception, catching the opponents at 13-13. It was a 1-point game until 20-19, then Leal scored an ace and Cantagalli, subbed in for the usual row exchange between setter and opposite, scored the set-winning block (25-21). Castellana started strong again (8-0!) in the 3rd but, unlike in the 1st, this time they managed to keep their lead until the end, winning it 25-17. 31% kills for Lube. The home team, then, started emulating their rivals. Castellana started 8-0 in the 3rd? We start 8-0 in the 4th! Perugia is winning games on serving? How many aces we had so far? 5? We score 6 in the 4th set alone! Grebennikov is defending everything? We name Balaso MVP of the match! Lube won the set 25-18 and the game 3-1. After all the troubles he had so far, great comeback game from Bruno (7 points, 6 aces). Castellana tried to snatch yet another point to a Scudetto contender with the usual blocking machine (12, 5 from Wlodarczyk, please forgive me, Polish friends, if I wrote it wrong) but Lube was too much for them.
Milano defended their 5th place in the standings with an easy win over Vibo (3-0). The match was a no-contest, ended with an aggregate 75-57 and with Milano recording 65% team kills, 28 break points in just 3 sets and giving away only 18 points, 15 of which on serving errors. Piano (8 points, 50% kills, 4 blocks) was the only player under 60% kills. Maar (6 points, 60% kills) took a break and watched Abdel-Aziz (16 points, 60% kills, 1 ace, 3 blocks) and Clevenot (17 points, 75% kills, 2 aces) destroy Vibo, who could only rely on the usual Al Hachadi (15 points, 54% kills, 1 ace). Kaziyski made his debut with his new team, as Verona hosted Latina. It was a tight match, with the guests winning the 1st after being down most of the set. The 2nd one was hard fought as well, with also a little beef between Boyer and Gitto, but this time Verona won it (28-26). The 3rd set was a little more comfortable for Verona (25-22), while the 4th one was a bloodbath for Latina (25-17). Nice debut by Kaziyski (21 points, 54% kills, 2 aces), well aided by Boyer (19 points, 46% kills, 1 block). Also, Grbic’s decision to take off Birarelli (1 point, 0% kills, 1 block) for Alletti (5 points, 67% kills, 1 ace) from the 2nd set onwards paid off. Stern (23 points, 50% kills, 2 aces) tried to impress his former club, but his effort was not matched by any of his teammates. Verona’s attempt to take the 6th place in the standings failed, though, because Monza was able to come back from Siena with 3 points (3-1). Siena gave all they could, ending with 57% positive reception, 49% team kills, 11 blocks (5 from Spadavecchia) and 4 men on double digits, but Monza was just better. Orduna orchestrated well the offense, recording 4 men on double digits as well and managing his hitters (20 for Ghafour, 17 for Plotnytski, 16 for Dzavoronok). After beating Perugia, Padova kept up the good work by easily disposing of Ravenna (3-0), which played an awful match (34% kills). Also, rumor has it that Ryley Barnes recovered from the injury that forced Lube to cut him this summer and will take Randazzo’s place in Padova.

2021/22 Italian women's Serie A1 - mid season recap and stats
I couldn’t follow the A1 femminile as thoroughly as I did with the men’s league, but since we’re halfway through regular season, let’s sum up what happened so far. First of all, here’s the standings:
Conegliano - 31 (11-1)
Novara - 28 (10-2)
Monza - 28 (9-3)
Scandicci - 26 (9-3)

Trento - 9 (2-10)

After quarterfinals, which have been seeded despite not all the andata matches were played, this will be the Italian Cup Final 4 schedule (all games will be live on both RaiSport and VBTV):
SEMIFINALS (January 5th):
Conegliano - Busto (4 pm)
Novara - Chieri (6.30 pm)
FINAL: January 6h, 5.30 pm
As you can see, there are no big surprises in the upper half of the standings. That is, if you don’t consider that one loss suffered by Conegliano as such. They lost a game after almost 2 years and after 76 straight wins (World record), and they did so in a strange way. It was a home match against a mid-table team (Firenze), and they were playing without Wolosz, De Kruijf and Plummer (other than Fahr, who had her ACL surgically rebuilt during the ECH and she will hopefully be back for the playoffs). Still, the team that won everything that was on the table in the last year and a half finally lost a match and, a couple weeks later, they suffered a much more sore defeat, when their arch-rivals Vakifbank Istanbul won another 5-setter in Ankara’s CWC final. It was Conegliano’s first defeat in a final match since the 2018/19 Champions League final, when Egonu still played for the other team. Also, this season the Panthers have been forced 3 more times to tie break, one of which against another mid-table team (Cuneo). They don’t look as unbeatable as before, but, as I wrote, they have suffered a lot of injuries and sometimes coach Santarelli was forced to make choices in order to comply with the Italians quota. They’re still the big favorites for the Scudetto, also because their contenders, as we say in Italy, are always 1 cent short of a Euro.
Let’s talk about Novara, for example. They had a big off-season, with the signing of Karakurt and a very deep roster, including a top scorer like Montibeller on the bench. Still, they keep choking on clutch games. When they faced Conegliano, they didn’t take advantage of the Panthers’ 27 errors in 3 sets, getting blocked 13 times and changing 3 lineups in 3 sets. It was a close one (25-22, 30-28, 25-23), but still a 3-0 defeat. Also, when they had the chance to reach them at the top, they had another 3-0 defeat against Scandicci, but this time much more neat (75-60). I think Novara’s main problem is Herbots’ health. The Belgium spiker never fully healed from that ECH abdomen injury and, while Daalderop has been a worthy alternative, she lacks the serving and spiking power of the former, which ultimately results in a distribution heavily skewed towards Karakurt. Their back row is extremely solid, though, as both Caterina Bosetti and Fersino are receiving really well and the latter is proving herself as one of the best liberos of the league on defense. What about Monza? 3 defeats so far, but only 1 worth 0 points (on match week 1, against Busto) and, most of all, a lot of injuries as well. Gennari and Mihajlovic were supposed to be the starting OHs, but they both barely played and, in their absence, coach Gaspari tried various solutions. The latest one was moving Stysiak to the left alongside Lazovic, and giving Van Hecke back her starting spot. Once they’ll have full roster, though, Monza will likely be a force to reckon with, as both Orro and Danesi are riding the ECH momentum and playing at a really high level. Scandicci had their fair share of injuries as well, but at least Merlo’s one was more than compensated with the signing of Castillo, who’s proving her worth even in such a competitive league. With such good passing, it’s no wonder that Malinov is having arguably the best season of her career, maybe feeling the duel with Orro for the starting position in NT. She’s managing a very balanced distribution, alternating the spikers, using the middles whenever possible and contributing with the occasional dump/spike (1.1 points/set with 59% kills). What’s Scandicci lacking for being at the top? Maybe a bit more consistency from Natalia and a bigger offensive contribution by Pietrini. It’s true that the talented Italian spiker is registering career highs in points/set, receiving efficiency and blocks/set, but also career lows in aces/set and kill %. She usually opts for a float serve, but as we saw last Summer, she’s also able to do a pretty powerful jump spin. If I was Barbolini (who’s from Modena like myself), I would encourage her to take some more risks from the line. This year, Busto Arsizio didn’t have to rush to compensate for a nightmare start like last season, and they’re right where they wanted to be, in the 4-team pack fighting for 2nd place, not even that far from Conegliano, and in the Italian Cup Final 4. Their firepower is prime, with both Mingardi and Gray among the top scorers and Olivotto having a great season so far. The Canadian spiker, in particular, is playing a terrific season, with Poulter often trusting her with clutch balls. They’re lacking a bit of back row work to be at the top, though, with neither Zannoni nor Lucia Bosetti being as solid as the Butterflies expected.
Talking about mid-table teams, Chieri so far has been able to replicate the great season they had last year. They kept most of their key players and they added a real gem in Cazaute. The former French league MVP is arguably the best “balanced spiker” of the league, as she’s the 2nd best OH for receiving efficiency and the 5th best OH for both kill % and blocks/set. Chieri might not have the overall talent to fight for a higher position, still they kicked Monza out of the Italian Cup with a pretty neat 3-0 road win. Then there’s Firenze, which, as I wrote, experienced the glory of defeating Conegliano. Other than that, the return of Sorokaite allowed Cambi to lighten the pressure on Nwakalor, who in turn answered with a great season. The long distance duel against Mingardi on who deserves to be Egonu’s reserve in NT is really firing up. Cuneo survived the Summer revolution pretty well, with the development of young players like Squarcini and Kuznetsova led by the experience of Signorile and Stufi. They forced both Conegliano and Monza to a tie break and they’re pretty much where they expected. Casalmaggiore, instead, was a pretty big surprise. They weren’t even sure they had the money to stay in A1 and their transfer season started really late, but in spite of that they’re now +4 on the relegation zone with 5 teams behind them. A really good result, considering their passing has been terrible and their starting libero is the league’s worst for receiving efficiency (20%).
Another team that is doing better than expected is Bergamo. Their situation was even worse than Casalmaggiore, and I predicted a Ravenna-like season for them. Instead, they’re leading the 5-teams pack that is fighting to avoid relegation. Lanier is pretty much buoying them, as she has to compensate for the fact that the signing of Borgo has been a pretty big bust. We’ll see how new signing Mackenzie May from UCLA will do in her 1st season as a pro. Vallefoglia finally found a “real” opposite in Bjelica, but, after a few good games at the beginning, she had some sloppy ones and they were back to a 3 OHs lineup, far less effective than the one in Trento’s men. Still, they seem to have found a real gem in Trinidad middle Jack-Sineal. Speaking of Trento, they’ve been pretty disappointing this season. The Piva bet failed miserably, as she’s been released and signed in A2, and Piani can’t carry the team every time. Relegation zone is only 1 point away, which is where Roma and Perugia are. The former were right in signing former Dynamo Moskva’s Klimets and middle Trnkova, but all the team has been so inconsistent that it’s no wonder they’re in the last spot. The latter, instead, had much higher hopes, but high-level signing Bongaerts was a real disappointment, as was Bauer’s Italian comeback. What really makes me sad, though, is watching Under 20 WCH MVP Guiducci rotting on the bench of such a dysfunctional team. I hope she’ll get some chances during the season.

Tl;dr protested a rule interpretation and won the protest, but it caused a significant delay, was a tight score in a semi-final match, was it worth the trouble?
I feel that I know the answer to the question that I am asking here, but just wondering what others think. Is it worth the hassle and time to protest a rule interpretation by a referee even if you know you'll "win" the protest? During a club tournament for 14U?
A common rule misinterpretation that a surprising number of refs seem to get wrong in youth volleyball is calling a setter for a backrow attack eventhough the ball is clearly contacted below the height of the net. My 4'9" setter isn't getting above the height of the net until trampolines become a part of the game. Some refs seem to equate jumping of a backrow player in front of the attack line with automatically being an illegal attack. Grinds my gears, but I have learned to just accept that an occasional ref has a loose understanding of the backrow attack rule.
Today my 14U team was playing in their regional championship tournament and had a situation occur twice with the same ref. The first time our setter chased a shanked dig that was heading out of play (off of the sport court surface). Our setter made a good play and kept the ball alive and another teammate played the ball over to keep the point alive. The ref blew the whistle and called the point for the other team. I did have our captain ask for an explanation and the ref said our setter had gone off the sport court. I didn't think our setter had, but it was close enough that I didn't dispute it. Also, it's a judgment call (if she had played the ball off the sport court surface or not), which can't be protested, so I didn't belabor the issue further. At that point we had a decent lead anyways. Whatever, move on, next point.
Next round it's a semi-final match with the same ref and the same situation occurs and this time the setter clearly plays the ball on the sport court playing surface and her momentum carried her off the court after playing the ball. The setter put up an amazing crosscourt backset and our OH pounded the ball. Ref blew the whistle and gave the point to the other team. I had the captain ask for an explanation and the ref said that the setter isn't allowed to travel off the sport court after playing the ball. I had my captain tell the ref that the setter can play the ball from the court and run right out the building if she wants. The ref said "safety issue", which is a valid rule in some other tournament specific rules, but not here. So I had the captain declare that we were officially protesting the interpretation of the rule and that the tournament officials need to be contacted. The ref has the scorers table go get the tournament officials. Then all of a sudden, when no one is ready she signals the other team to serve! Boom, ace. And now I'm like wtf, and I again have my captain ask why are we playing on with the other team serving without getting the rule protest decided. The ref says that we're going to keep playing until the tournament officials come and decide what's up with the rule interpretation protest. I'm not having it. We shouldn't be proceeding until the rule issue is resolved. And if anything it should still be our serve.
Anyways, the tournament officials come and straighten it out. They take off the bonus sneak attack serve point, we replay the point regarding the rule interpretation with us serving. The right decision within the rules.
But here's the thing. Yes the match was close, 16-14, in a semi-final match, but the delay of protesting and getting the tournament officials involved and them sorting through it all took at least 15 minutes. We ended up winning the set 25-23, so by virtue of the points that would've been lost had I not had the rule interpretation protested it could have cost us the set and potentially the match. At the same time though, is arguing points in a youth volleyball game ever really worth it? Our court was already almost an hour behind. Is adding another 15 or 20 minutes to that by officially arguing worth it?

text:
After three weeks and way too many games of volleyball, the men’s world championships are over. Lots of amazing volleyball was played, many highlights made the rounds on Instagram, and most Bulgarians stayed home for matches. As for the results, Drake put it best: “Back-to-back like I’m Jordan ’96 ’97 whoa”. Congratulations to Poland for an impressive two world championships gold medals in a row. And to Brazil for the silver, the USA for the bronze, and to the rest for trying their best. We get the women’s tournament back-to-back as well! My team is almost out of it 3 days into the tournament though. Alas, because I haven’t scratched my writing itch in a while, here is ~1500 words on what this Canadian thought of the 2018 men’s edition of the tournament.
1. Unfortunately, my first thought is going to be negative. And if you have followed my podcast or videos, you probably know what it is going to be. The tournament format. This is something that is not hard to get right. For most sporting events, the structure is barely a blip on the radar of things to complain about. But the World Championships was severely hampered by strange, complicated, and frustrating decisions about how teams advance.
• The initial pools were based on horribly outdated team rankings, making the first group stage imbalanced. Poland, our eventual champions, and Italy coasted through an easy first group while France, Canada, and Brazil had a brutal initial stage to deal with. This issue was compounded by the fact that points carried over from these uneven 1st groups in the second stage. France beat our gold medalists relatively convincingly in the second round and didn’t advance to the final 6!
• The final 6. No matter what you think of the other format complaints, this is something everyone wants to get rid of. Because this out third round of pool play, we had meaningless games two days before the tournament finals. TWO DAYS. The Brazil and USA benches played each other, and Serbia didn’t care against Poland on a forgettable Friday. This is when the tension of the tournament should be ramping up, not sputtering out. Get rid of the final 6 that no other sport uses for a good reason, and at least implement an 8-team single elimination bracket.
• Too many matches. This one is more for the players, who must endure a grueling gauntlet of volleyball right before the start of their club seasons. With 12 games in such a short period, injury risk increases, and exhaustion becomes a factor. Teams really started to lose steam by the final 6, lowering the quality of play. Even as a die-hard fan it is impossible to watch every game I wanted to. Lowering the number of matches in the tournament would be a benefit to both fans and players.
2. Kurek is a beast. Holy crap that was an impressive performance in the final round. 20/29 attacking in the championship game is one of the most impressive performances of all time in a World Championship final. Almost unprecedented for a guy who we weren’t even sure was going to start at the beginning of the tournament. Just an amazing redemption story.
After being left off the gold medal team in 2014, then mailing in several disappointing club seasons, it was easy to write him off as a gifted athlete whose attitude would always hold them back. Seriously, for anyone who watched him in Ziraat Bankasi Ankara last year, he looked like he was ready to quit volleyball. Kurek’s World Championship MVP must be incredibly validating for him and I hope we get to see this Bartosz Kurek more often.
3. The production of the event could be so, so much better. Where are the pre and post-game shows? Where are announcers who know what they are talking about? Where is the analysis that goes beyond basic post-game recaps? Especially now that we are paying $20 to watch the tournament. Watching volleyball for the love of the game is great, but so much of what makes sports entertaining are the storylines that surround the players and teams. Just going from what the broadcast and website provided, you would have no context behind anything that happened in the tournament.
4. The level of volleyball in this tournament was amazingly high. We are watching the best generation of volleyball players ever, and they are only getting better. I don’t want to disrespect the players who laid the foundation for the modern game, but watching video from the 1972 Olympic Games, it barely looks like the same sport. Even the progress since the early 2000s has been astounding. There is still a lot of room left to grow in terms of both skills, athleticism, and tactics, but you are guaranteed at least one mind-blowing play every set. The fact that the quality of play on the court is so high makes all my complaints about format and production even more frustrating.
5. I already touched on this, but it deserves its own bullet point. We need better announcers! This isn’t golf, we shouldn’t have a British dude making 1-2 comments per minute about what they see in front of them. Look at big conference women’s NCAA games to see how much more enjoyable watching volleyball is when you have a knowledgeable and engaging 2-person commentary booth. Especially when you have so much downtime between timeouts, challenges, and missed serves. There are so many people who would be awesome in the booth and really improve the viewing experience.
6. There is no way I would have thought we would be having a Brazil vs Poland championship game rematch. Any final that didn’t involve one of the USA, France, or Russia seemed unlikely at the start of the tournament. Brazil was missing both its starting outside hitters in Ricardo Lucarelli and Mauricio Borges, and Poland had suffered many disappointments in the international stage since their 2014 world championship win.
But I think it's awesome that it is so hard to make predictions. We’re spoiled with contenders at the men’s senior level. Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Poland, Russia, Serbia, and the USA all could have won medals had a couple of balls gone a different way. I’m sure we’ll see different medalists at next summer’s VNL and World Cup.
7. Following the game threads on reddit was one of my favourite volleyball-watching experiences in a while. Especially in the final round when we got contributions from a wide variety of fans. We’ve seen the concept become extremely successful for the NBA, NFL, and NHL so it makes sense that it works well for a sport with lots of breaks like volleyball. I think reddit, in general, is the best second-screen experience in sports, and I hope the game threads continue for the women’s world championships and this year’s club season.
8. Volleyball is still in the stone age when it comes to stats. We are just approaching the conclusion that most sports leagues arrived at in the 90s, which is that numbers tell us a lot about the game. The only mention of stats by the FIVB broadcast or website is when point, block, or ace records are close to being broken. I want to know if Filippo Lanza forcing opponents into poor passing situations with his serve. I want to know what outsides are hitting against Sharone Vernon-Evans in single block situations. I want to know the % difference between Taylor Sander and Aaron Russell as pipe hitters. This is a lot to ask, but it shouldn’t be. But for now, can we please get stats as per set in addition to totals.
9. I swear wipes go off the attacking player’s hand last half the time, but I have yet to see it called in the defense’s favour. This move was a point of emphasis by the FIVB but is still officiated inconsistently in my opinion.
10. If you liked watching this tournament but are sad that volleyball is over until next summer, you are in luck! The pro season is about to start, and the Italian League is looking more stacked than ever. There is also the Champions League, Russian League, Polish League, and Brazilian League with many high-level players and teams. Pick one team and become a fan! In many ways, I prefer watching the club season to international play. The slower pace makes it easier to follow and storylines develop more organically over the course of 8 months. I’ll be releasing a guide on how to follow and watch pro volleyball this season sometime next week. And maybe be doing a fantasy volleyball league so if you are interested in that let me know.

The International Dream Team (best team in the world using players from various nationalities)
Inspired by u/paninoislove's Top 5 Players at Each Position post, I want to discuss the best team you could possibly form in the international scene right now.
Here's a quick rundown:
Setter: Micah Christenson
One of the new trailblazers in the up and coming tall dynamic setter bunch, Micah Christenson leads the setter world with his amazing blocks, serves, and sets. He's also not half bad at defense. Boasting a 6'6 height and a nasty funky flat serve which he can turn into a hybrid, Micah Christenson is one of the best all round setters with one of the craziest set-kill percentages out there.
Outside Hitter 1: Wilfredo Leon
I mean, come on. We all knew this guy was going to be here. Boasting possibly one of the most powerful serves to ever exist on the planet, Wilfredo Leon is a beast, being capable of putting almost every ball away. He can also save a ball or two, having some great defense on the court. He's basically carrying Sir Perugia in the Italian Superleague as of now.
Outside Hitter 2: Yoandy Leal
Not far behind from his other Cuban relative, Yoandy Leal snatches the second outside hitter spot. Just like Leon, he has one of the strongest serves in the world right now. He's also capable of putting the ball away in enormous numbers. Having a strong serve, a strong spike, and a strong receive, Leal is a player you simply cannot ignore.
Opposite Hitter: Nimir Abdel-Aziz
The setter who made a switch to the opposite position, this captain of the Netherlands is a beast. Having a godlike kill percentage and an insane ace percentage to boot, he basically carries any team he's on: even more than that, he can act as a second setter due to his sheer skill at both positions.
Middle Blocker 1: Robertlandy Simon
Another Cuban player, the 6'10 middle has a serve comparable to Leon's, being the hardest server of the bunch in Lube Civitanova. Playing against Simon is like trying to play a game against a hacker: you simply cannot win. The man was gifted by God to become one of the best volleyball middle blockers out there, and he takes the crown. Boasting insane kill, ace, and block percentages, Robertlandy Simon is simply someone you do not want to play against.
Middle Blocker 2: Dmitriy Muserskiy
The 7'2ft/218 cm Russian middle blocker needs no explanation. Having the height of a giant, Muserskiy is a freak of nature who was simply not meant to play the game. Utilizing his height to bring down the hammer on his jump serve, he's also able to hit a sizeable amount of aces. Needless to say, he is simply unfair at blocking due to his height.
Libero: Jenia Grebennikov
The living highlight reel, Grebennikov needs no explanation. Being able to save the most impossible of balls (even from the giants in this list here) is a trivial task for him. Also having a great emergency set, Grebennikov's placement is more than justified.

Setter: Bruno Rezende, Saeid Marouf

Opposite Hitter: Maxim Mikhaylov, Matt Anderson
Middle Blocker: Lucas Saatkamp, Max Holt

So this happens to me a lot, and I'm wondering how everyone handles this problem during games. I play volleyball casually, and I would say that my serves and receives have gotten better over time. Today, however, I find myself overthinking which serve I have to use as we were down by a lot of points in the 2nd set. Because I prefer to be at peace duing my service attempts, I signed my teammate, who's ordering me to do a simple underhand serve, to keep quiet so I could concentrate. He got angry and told me he was just coaching me, which threw me off my focus and led me to fail at doing my overhand serve, which at the time was doing well.
After failing that serve, I also started losing my focus on positioning for receives. Add to that is the stress of my teammates who are constantly getting annoyed even though they would also stray out of their positions during rallies. Knowing that this set is over for us, I quit before the final point is taken since I was also getting annoyed at how we're playing the game, even if it's just for fun.
We tried another set after, but I switched teams (we're workmates so there's no trouble in that) and they assured me that I won't be as stressed out as I did with the other team. Sure enough, they're certainly better, less selfish, and more patient with me during the next set. I even got back at the other team with a dump, a service ace from an underhand serve which my previous teammate advised me to do, and, most importantly, 2 overhand service aces that they don't want me doing when I was on their team!
I guess it realy helps when your team is patient and understanding with you, especially during serves when you're basically alone attacking on the court. Going back though, maybe I did annoy my teammate for shushing him, but the loudness and teasing during my serves were even heard before I did that. I did not regret using an overhand serve at all, nor will I ever regret doing it. My serves will be inconsistent, but that's just because that's how difficult serving can be. But I will never stop at anything if it doesn't work at first, because I know for certain that with enough practice, my serves will be as good as I want it to be in the end.

text:
I’m interested in how every one classifies different levels of play and what caveats need to be made. If you have any experience in doing this any resources or examples would be really appreciated.
In the country where I’m at there are 5 levels, Beginner, lower intermediate, mid intermediate, upper intermediate and advanced. I recently saw a post by Kody Kessel on how USAV Performance ranks their athletes. I’ve posted below how they have been described by one of the leading social/rec organizations, and something feels off to me. Looking forward to your input as I’m trying to put together my own courses.
Lower-Intermediate ability level You should:
Understand the importance of using 3 touches in play (Receive, Set, Hit)
Have control of your momentum and land safely on your side of the court after going up for a hit.
Attempt the 3 step approach and try to attack with threat
Understand that every player serves a specific role on the court. For example, a receiver passes to the setter, who usually has the second touch to set, but can also shout for help from the team.
Understand that if you're in the back court you cannot jump and hit from the front court (inside the 3m line).
Be able to overhand or underhand serve the ball over the net and in play 60% of the time or higher.
Pass to your teammates most of the time, but sometimes just hit the ball back over the net. Hit or push the ball over the net, trying to keep it in bounds, not necessarily trying to place it strategically.
Know what blocking is and attempt to do so safely but don’t see a lot of it at your level of play.
Know when to call for the ball to avoid collisions
Know that you cannot touch the net at any point in time.
Receive the ball from a serve well but not perfectly with the aim to pass to the setter, and are starting to receive more difficult serves.
Have decent fundamentals of receiving/passing, setting & spiking but still have a lot of room for improvement.
Mid-Intermediate ability level You should:
Have a thorough understanding of the volleyball rules and the different tactics involved.
Begin to play to your personal strengths and choose a position to play in the 5:1 formation (i.e. outside, opposite, setter etc.)
Be able to pass well and consistently, with most of your passes going to the setter so they can set to one of the hitters.
Be able to set well enough for a hitter to hit Understand what covering a hitter means Be able to receive/dig some more difficult hits/spikes
Attempt and be able to block hitters from the opposing team
Mainly serve overhand and get more than 70% of your serves in play/get some ace serves.
Overall your fundamentals of receiving/passing, setting & spiking should be solid and good enough to maintain a good competitive rally.
Upper-Intermediate ability level
You should:
Know all the technical rules of the game.
Have a thorough understanding of different types of sets to each hitter (Quick, Pipe, Slide, Shoot, Different Tempos etc.)
Be able to serve to a zone regularly, sometimes jump serve accurately. Be able to receive more difficult serves and pass to the setter
Understand how to run a 5-1 and 6-2 positions and know/play at least 2 different positions (Outside, Middle, Opposite, Libero, Setter)
Know how to cover the court defensively during a serve and during a hit.
Get 90% of serves, or more, in play.
Your fundamentals of receiving/passing, setting, and spiking are very good and you can play in competitive games.
Likely have experience or can play in an official competitive volleyball league

text: Hi guys, since I've nothing more interesting to do (despite being 3A.M. and having an exam in a few days) I decided to write this long poem to help the ones of you that struggle with jumping. First of all (since someone might need to hear it) you don't need to be 2 meters tall and jump 110cm to be good at volleyball. Sure that gives you an edge but its definitely not everything, so don't obsess too much on it. With that settled let's begin. I'll dump a lot of knowledge on you from someone who spent an unhealthy amount of time trying to optimize his technique. Let's understand what allows us to jump. There's this little thing called gravity that keeps us anchored to the ground. To jump we need to overcome the gravitational pull exerting enough explosive power. If you've studied some physics we can get a couple of things from that. The force on you by gravity is 9.81x your body weight. Which means the higher the weight the higher the force needed. In other words "fat dont fly". Before you starve yourselves to death keep in mind that you still need to be strong. Ideally you'd want to be in the 12-15% of body fat to optimize performance. A little more isn't necessarily an issue but don't expect to be like Nishida if you are at 30%. I want to introduce you to the "Law of specificity". If you want to be good at something you gotta do that thing. A real shocker I know but it is more interesting than Just that. The thing is that jumping is self progressing as itself. When doing any exercise you need to progress overtime to improve, challenging yourself with a greater stimulus. Well jumping already does that. Because my jumping more you'll get more stimulus when landing. And that is self fueling. That's why you can have freaky jumpers who never stepped in a gym to lift weights once in their life. Yes they are also genetic freaks and not everyone is gifted like that. For most people the ceiling is way lower if you are not doing anything more. What jumping gives you is two other things, first is neural adaptation. Your body becomes more efficient recruiting the muscle fibers required, making you jump higher. The other this is the ability to put intent. If you don't put intent into your jumps or lifts you'll never, ever, ever jump higher. You can become freakishly strong but lose jump (I talk from experience). That's extremely important especially for younger athletes. Now we get to the lifting part. Do you remember the freaky jumpers who never touched a weight I mentioned earlier? Good, you are not senile yet. They jumped that high without proper training, which means that could have jumped even more. That's what you are going to do. At first I want you to focus on getting stronger. I want you to get your legs as strong as physically possible. Squat. Squat as your life depended on it. Don't chase numbers tho. Learn the proper technique. And even if you have perfect technique don't chase the numbers. Well you should chase them but not the weight. Weight is not the right number to chase. And you might think "you told me I should get stronger and yet I shouldn't chase the weight? You are just saying random stuff". Fair. At which I ask you to remember the little physics lesson I gave you earlier. You need you be able to generate force fast. Which means you have to be able to move heavy weights fast. My advice is to get to 1.5 of your body weight of a back squat as a PR, then pick a weight you can do 3 to 5 reps with and do singles trying to move it as fast as possible. (There are many apps to track bar speed) Don't cheat depth. ATG all the way. If you don't have the mobility work for it. Mobility is another big limitation for jumping. Another very important exercise is a power clean. Very hard to learn but so rewarding. You'll get the ability to learn complex skills and train RFD (rate of force development) in an unmatched way. They are gonna look very bad for a very long time but trust me, still worth it to do and learn. They don't need to be perfect to work but the better the technique the more weight you can move the more adaptation you get. Don't underestimate your calves, they deserve some love too. Train them heavy. Very heavy. You'll be surprised how resilient of a muscle they are. While doing all of that don't forget to keep jumping. If you don't play volleyball for a period (maybe in off season or something like that) do some jumping sessions. Max effort jumps. However you like them. That could be dunking, spiking,...Get your jumping technique dialed in. That can be four, three or two steps (this is recommended especially for middles but it's useful when blocking in any position). Your jump technique is what you use to convert your speed into height. You approach full speed and that makes you jump higher. Your penultimate step needs to be long. And not just for the sake of it. The goal is to get lower. By getting lower you get more time to exert force into the ground and explode upward. Your last step is the block step. Turn it sideways to brake you. A common error I see is putting your brake foot too close to where you planted your penultimate. That is gonna cost you a lot of cm. Trust me. Also even if you are short, you should start your penultimate before the 3 meters line. Watch Isaiah Espinoza if you need reference (one of the best jumpers in the world, on the shorter side). Don't underestimate your arms. They add a lot to your vert. You need to swing them backwards and then very aggressively forward. They should go in front of you the exact moment you takeoff. Honestly, I could rumble about for forever, I'm happy to go into more details for everyone that wants it. Even give you gym suggestions. I think I have to specify that I'm not a certified coach or personal trainer. I'm just talking from my personal experience and research

This is a tall volleyball player’s rant. I’m relatively tall, and my original position is OH. I join various private teams and drop-ins to enjoy volleyball, but most players—especially shorter ones—insist on playing OH, or OP if OH isn’t available, saying they can’t play MB because they’re too short. The thing is, players who can only do OH or OP usually aren’t that skilled, so the serve receive breaks down, it’s nothing but out-of-system sets to the left or right, and on top of that, they often mess up those sets. As a result, I barely get any chance to spike, and we end up losing because the OHs or OPs keep making errors.
Honestly, since OH is the position that touches the ball the most, I feel it makes way more sense to put the most technically skilled player there, and stick the less skilled, shorter players at MB. Every time, I can’t help but feel frustrated. (Of course, I’m not talking about pro-level volleyball here.)

text:
Becoming a good volleyball player is like being a Jedi. Patience, honing skills and persistence bring you far, rage, anger and impatience will make it worse.
Reading in this r/ is always an interesting thing. It brings a lot of people together, across all genders and ages.
A lot of posts are circling around the topic "I'm frustrated because I didn't make the team" or "How do I improve?"
As someone who participates in this sport for over 25 years, I'd like to give the younger folks here some advice:
1. Volleyyball is 20% Talent, 30% sweat, blood and tears, and 50% time. It takes a lot of time to get an idea of the ideal techniques, positional play and awareness on the court.
2. Learn from peers, learn from folks that has been playing longer than you have, no matter to age and gender.
3. Be patient. Your time will come. Do not feel bad when you are benched, take the opportunity to observe your counterpart and analyze the opponent for mistakes that you can exploit when it is your turn to enter the court.
4. Be persistent. Use the practice to become better. Take those 250 services, and with each you will get a better idea of how to use it for yourself as an advantage.
5. Time will make you a good player. It takes a few years to be good enough at the basic skills. Then the advanced skills will get you. Do not fear the time it takes to become good.
6. Be frustrated. But turn that energy into the will to improve. The more you work on yourself (on and off the court) the better you will become.
7. Gear does not make you a good player. Playing makes you a good player.
8. Make mistakes. Make a lot of them. Learn from them. Then make even more.
9. There is no easy path to follow. Volleyball is the ultimate team sport, it breathes team play: There is no attack possible without at least one player helping you. There is no I, there is no you; only your team. Grow together, learn from each other.
10. Be bold. Go for the kill, go for the dive. Do not try, do. How else will you get better?
I know it is hard to be patient, to be told by someone to take a step back. But know this:
Your Time Will Come. And You Will Be Ready.
label: hot_take

I'll start - The net calls in indoor should be significantly loosened. The way I see it, net calls should only be called if 1) they genuinely interfere with play, or 2) the net touch is genuinely dangerous. But the rule has evolved into penalising literally any contact on the net, no matter how small. Simply brushing the net with a finger which has no effect on play and doesn't put anyone in harm's way shouldn't be illegal.
Edit: I don't think I worded this to my intention - I don't mean net calls when hitting or blocking. I mean ones where like for example the other team is completely out of system and far from the net and no attack is likely and then someone brushes the net with their fingertips and it gets called.
